QDS K1848 2.2.67.
A FASHION SHOW WAS HELD BY THE MINISTRY
OF PUBLIC BUILDING AND WORKS IN LONDON TODAY
TO TRY TO PERSUADE BUILDERS THAT THEY NEED
NOT HALT WORK DURING WINTRY WEATHER.
WINTER WEAR FOR BUILDING WORKMEN,
EVOLVED BY OFFICIALS AND CLOTHING DESIGNERS,
WAS DISPLAYED AT THIS NOVEL KIND OF FASHION
SHOW.

(LEFT-RIGHT) A BASIC TWO-PIECE
SUIT; MADE IN PROOFED NYLON, WITH EXTENSIVE
VENTING AND ADJUSTABLE SLEEVE AND TROUSER
CUFFS; A BASIC SUIT MADE IN A NEW PLASTIC/
TERY LENE LAMINATE MATERIAL WHICH IS CLAIMED
TO BE BOTH PERMEABLE AND WATERPROOF; A BASIC
NYLON SUIT WITH A HOOD IN PLACE OF THE NORMAL
JACKET COLLAR; AND A NEW TYPE OF DONKEY
JACKET MADE OF A LAMINATE COTTON, FOAM AND
RUBBER WOOL.

         BRITAINS BIGGEST WHEATFIELD

What is believed to be the biggest field of wheat in
Britain, a 400 acre block, which had not felt the
plough for 20 years and was practically derelict, is
now being out high up on the Sussex Downs.
The field is expected to produce about 17 cwt. of
grain an acre, and 40 Australian binders, handled by
land girls, are harvesting the corn.

Photo shows:- A typical study of a land girl on a
binder cutting the huge wheatfield.

        1 8 FEB 1960
        DAILY HERA
        PROPERTY O

FROM BLACK OF READING

The Duke of Edinburgh's new Harvard training plane gets the five-stars
insignia of Marshal of the Royal Air Force after delivery to White Waltham
(Berks) R.A.F. station.
Pictured here putting the finishing touches to the job is Fairey Aviation
mechanic Peter Barton of Gosbrook Road, Caversham, Reading. With him is
Sgt. James Murray, one of the ground staff who will service the plane.
Delivery of the 200-miles-an-hour American-built Harvard means that the
Duke's training has now progressed beyond the 120 m.p.h. Chipmunk in which
he received his initial flying lessons. When he masters the Harvard, he
will move on to jet planes - probably the 600-miles-an-hour Gloster Meteor.

end

This is a pilot observation report.
The group size is 12 men.
This is probably a training exercise.
The men are wearing green fatigue uniforms.
All of them are wearing tin hats.
The men are exercising in a wooded area.
All of the men appear to be in good health.
The men are seen to be using the following equipment.
(1) A light machine gun, model 1919 A4.
(2) A light machine gun, model 1918 A2.
(3) A sub-machine gun, model Thompson.
(4) A rifle, model M1 Garand.
(5) A rifle, model Springfield.
(6) A bazooka.
The men are in good spirits and are seen to be enjoying themselves.

PROGRESS ON THE ANGLO-
The great new oil refinery of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company,
with a projected capacity of 4,000,000 tons a year, is taking
shape. It is due for completion in the summer of 1952,
but the Crude Oil Distillation Unit and its necessary
auxiliaries are expected to be in commission in a few months.
Situated at the Isle of Grain, on the Kent coast, the new
refinery will cost £40,000,000, and its output will be about
one-sixth of the Abadan refinery. It is being constructed
on reclaimed marshland on which a million tons of sand from
the sea bed off the Nore have been pumped in order to stop
the natural sinking of the land, and to prevent the sand
drifting, a mixture of grass and clover has been planted.
New jetties are under construction to accommodate the largest
of tankers, and there will be 160 storage tanks.
The picture shows:

1983-5286/51756

A view of the new refinery site looking south-east from
Cat. Cracker, showing combined blow down stack and tanks
in the foreground, Crude Distillation Unit (left centre),
No.1 Vacuum Unit (right centre), temporary construction
Offices, canteen, concrete batch plant, etc. Centre
background. River seen in far distance.

Indus, Oil Refineries, Isle of Grain.

" A MILLION WOMEN MUST COME INTO OUR WAR INDUSTRY -- "
Following Mr. Churchill's dramatic speech, this picture
is of particular interest. He stated that more than a
million women must come forward into our war industry,
into the shell plants, and ammunition works. This picture
was taken at the Paddington Technical Institute, where a
number of Women Engineers are undergoing training. No
doubt many of them will be playing their part in this
war with some valuable work on the home front.

Photo shows- A study of one of the women engineers under
instruction at the Paddington Technical Institute.

        They Planned A City

Even while Nazi bombs were raining on London, experts with their eyes fixed
on the future, were planning a new London that shall do away with the
many blemishes that still mar the face of the Empire's capital. Now you are
introduced to some of the people who have been working for the future of
London in this article by CONNERY CHAPPELL

OHN HENRY FORSHAW, M.C., the ex-Royal
Engineers officer, who is the chief man behind
the London County Council's Plan for rebuild-
ing London, is forty-seven and earns £2,750 a year.
And while the Plan, to which he contributed more
than any one else has had more space and publicity
than any other single news item since the war started,
Forshaw himself has had practically none. Which is
how he prefers it.

The Plan, of course, has broken all records. It has
gone into a second edition as a book at 12s. 6d. More
than 1,500 people a day have seen models of it at the
County Hall—mostly housewives, service men on
leave and young people who wanted to see the world
of the future—there its exhibition has had to be ex-
tended. Editorial comment on it runs into hundreds
of columns.

In short, after taking two years to prepare, the Plan
is revealed as the biggest thing of its type ever at-
tempted.

It is a Plan, not of lines, but of lives, designed to
take the ugliness out of London, in the words of Lord
Latham, Leader of the Council.
The decision to produce it was taken more than two
years ago, during the big air raids. A special staff
was built up from people in the Town Planning Sec-
tion of the L.C.C.'s big architectural department at
County Hall.
Every one concerned with it carried on with their

normal Civil Defence and Home Guard duties, and
often with their departmental work as well. There were
no privileges, no special favours. It was an enormous
job, frequently done under bad conditions during air
raids.

As consultant, the L.C.C. engaged Leslie Patrick
Abercrombie, Professor of Town Planning at Uni-
versity College, London, who is accepted as Britain's
leading expert on the subject. Wesley Dougill, who
died in February, when the job was nearly done, was
Assistant Planning Officer, and did brilliant work.

The whole thing was produced on an informal con-
ference system, many meetings taking place in the
early hours of the morning during the hectic nights of
1941.

Professor Abercrombie, who was visiting County
Hall several times a week, frequently stayed over and
slept there, and Mr. Forshaw was usually on the spot—
for in addition to his position as deputy architect and
later architect to the council he was also in charge of
A.R.P. rescue work and debris disposal for London.

This involved spending many nights at headquarters
and it was during these sessions, waiting for air raid
alerts, that a lot of the early theoretical work was done.

Gradually, the staff sorted itself out; it never
exceeded thirty and averaged about twenty. It was
enthusiastic, and young, which was as well, for an
enormous amount of groundwork had to be cleared up
before the Plan could reach the drawing boards.
Consultations at what the council calls “officer

    —4 SEP. 1943

Mr. Cassells, about M.P. for Dunbartonshire, has informed the secretary of the Scottish Labour Party of his intention to retire at the next General Election.

J. Parkes, of Blackpool, received fatal injuries yesterday when the collapse of a water main trench at South Shore, Blackpool, buried him up to his head and shoulders.

Jarrow Town Council has decided to promote a Bill in Parliament to give it powers to acquire land by agreement or compulsion for industrial purposes and to advance money for buildings.

The Board of Trade announce that a draft Order-in-Council was laid before Parliament on November 22 requiring imported solid-headed pins of brass, iron, or steel to bear an indication of origin.

More than a dozen skeletons were found during excavation for a new cinema at Devizes. They were examined by Captain B. Howard Cunnington, the Wiltshire archaeologist, who said they were of no archaeological value.

Trooper Edward Williams, 4th/7th Dragoon Guards, stationed at Aldershot, died yesterday in the Cambridge Military Hospital, Aldershot. Riding an Army motor-cycle on Tuesday, he came into collision with an Army light tank.

Mr. F. A. Soden, assistant foreman in the L.M.S. erecting shop, Crewe, has been chosen to accompany the company's Coronation engine on its tour of the United States next year; it will be shown at the World's Fair in New York.

At Nottingham yesterday Joseph Hardstaff, the Nottinghamshire and England cricketer, was fined Ã‚Â£10 and ordered to pay Ã‚Â£1 3s. 6d. costs for driving a motor-car in a dangerous manner. His licence was endorsed. He pleaded "Not Guilty."

After refusing for a number of years to send a member to represent the Borough on the Essex Territorial Army Association, West Ham Town Council on Tuesday night decided to reverse its previous decision. The Labour Party selected Councillor A. G. Schnn as a representative and he was elected.

Mrs. Sydney Marsham has been appointed chairman of the executive committee of the Imperial Council of the Girl Guides Association, in the place of Dame Helen Gwynne-Vaughan, who has resigned. Lady Clarendon has been appointed vice-chairman in the place of Mrs. Charles Tufton, who has resigned.

The motor lifeboat which was on view in the lifeboat pavilion at the Empire Exhibition, Glasgow, for six months, leaves the Clyde today, after final adjustments, to take up her real work at Tobermory, Isle of Mull. The boat has cost about Ã‚Â£8,000 and is a gift to the Royal National Life-boat Institution from Miss Margaret Lithgow, of Glengorm Castle, Tobermory, who died a few weeks ago.

THE FUR STORAGE
VAULT
wavy.
By CALLISTHENES

The other day a charming customer
who brought to our Fur Department
several articles requiring immediate
attention told us of an experience which
may be common to many. Last Spring,
feeling very economical and imagining
that the trifling cost of fur storage might
be avoided, the lady purchased a moth-
proof bag, stored her furs therein and
put the bag away. The receptacle,
unfortunately, was not proof against
the tiny invader, for a carelessly folded
opening admitted the enemy, with the
result that the lady’s furs can only be
saved by the immediate attention we
are now giving them. For protection
is not so much a matter of only moth-
proof bags as the application of storage
conditions that make damage
impossible.

The Fur Storage Vault of ours is a
well-known and enormously patronised
department of this business. We believe
it to be one of the largest fur vaults
of its kind in the world. It is so arranged
that its temperature is maintained
continuously below freezing-point, so
that it becomes impossible for moth
eggs to germinate, even though they be
depply hidden in the fur. But this
precaution against germination is only
a single stage in a carefully planned
campaign against the insinuating moth.
Two or three times during the summer
months—for an entire 24 hours—the
temperature of the vault is allowed to
rise to that of the street. By this means
whatever eggs are left in the furs are
encouraged to hatch out. The trouble-
some insects are then submitted to the
freezing process and eliminated utterly.
It has been noted, by the way, that pelts
treated by this process recover their
original sheen, and seem rejuvenated
after their emergence from cold storage.
Carefully examined before they are
stowed away and no less carefully
re-examined before being handed over,
the pelts return with a newness and a
glossiness which is otherwise lost to
them. The cost of this work is so
small—a matter, really, of a few shillings
—as to represent the most profitable
outlay on one’s wardrobe needs.

We have now arrived at a period of the
year when many of these gems of the furrier's
art are being removed. Yet we feel that our
reference to this fascinating subject is timely,
if only for the moral it points. To incur
avoidable risk to precious furs in the hope
of saving a few shillings for storage is to be
“ penny wise, pound foolish ” in the widest
sense of the phrase.

Selfridge & Co., Ltd.

239513       BRIN
TORY M.P.s TAKE T.V. COURSE.


London: Mr. Charles Orr-Ewing, Conservative
Member of Parliament for Hendon, North, sits
in the camera chair when fourteen Conservative
members of Parliament to-day began a B.B.C.
television course, similar to one recently held
for television writers, at Alexandria Palace.
The M.P.'s accepted an invitation from Mr. George
Barnes, the television director, to see something
of technique requirements and production problems
from the inside.
A number of Socialists are also to take the course
at the end of this month.
3rd. October, 1952 PN-d.

NOT so long ago nearly
everybody thought
that they knew the
answer to the traffic prob-
lem.

We had only to spend a
few hundred millions a year
on motorways, ring roads,
flyovers, road widenings and
multi-storey parking
garages, and Bob would (in
due course) be your uncle.
This innocent illusion, because
successive Governments have
refused to spend anything more
than small change on building
roads, and we were unable to
learn from experience (as the
Americans are now doing) that
the engineering solution opens a
bottomless financial pit, but

—the futuristic town

planned to make

the best of motors

by
Malcolm MacEwen

an official of the Royal Institute of British Architects

does not solve the traffic
problem.
Two cars in every Los
Angeles garage are a sign less
of American affluence than of
the catastrophic collapse of
public transport, of waste on a
vast scale, and of the dispersal
of the city far and wide over
the countryside.
“Motopia” is the name given

by G. A. Jellicoe, the landscape
architect, architect and town-
planner, to his theoretical
design for an ideal motorised
town.

Its great merit is that he
breaks through the fetters of
conventional thinking in an
effort to design a new kind of
town in which we can get the
best of both worlds — the
mobility of the motor car with-
out its dirt, noise, smells, con-
estion and danger.

Motopia consists of a rect-
angular grid of five-storey ter-
races, forming a series of great
own “squares.”

The first four storeys are flats
and maisonettes, some with gar-
lens; the fifth storey is a
“mews storey” for car parking
and vehicular access; and the
roads are on the roof, screened
by plants.

The entire space between the
buildings, and under them, is a
vast park of unending variety
and beauty, in which lie schools
and other public buildings, and
through which one can walk
everywhere in safety.

At the corner of each square
the buildings form a hollow
circle, containing local shops
and other facilities on the
ground floor, and a roundabout
for the rooftop road.

SHOPPING

At one side of the town is a
great multi-level, glassed-in
shopping centre, where people
meet for shopping and pleasure
after parking their cars on the
roof.

It is easy to criticise Mr. Jel-
licoe’s conception. It is a shot
in the dark because nobody has
yet done the basic studies on
traffic generation that would
enable us to discover the practi-
cal limits to the use of the motor
car in towns.

All we do know is that large
towns and cities, if they are to

“Helicopter-view” of

space that would normally
be taken up by congested
roads is given over to parks
and recreation grounds.

remain reasonably compact
groupings for social intercourse,
must depend largely on public
transport.
In Motopia, this is limited to
water buses on the lakes—
delightful, but of limited prac-
tical value.

To put the traffic on the roof
and the people on the ground is
obviously more difficult than the
opposite, and the widths of
roads and roundabouts are
limited by the width of the
buildings, and cannot easily be
related to the volume of traffic.

EXERCISE

To dismiss Motopia for these
reasons would, however, be to
miss its real point. For Motopia
is an exercise in the imagina-
tion, and opens our eyes to the
possibilities that have still to be
explored in landscape and town
design.

The greater part of the book
illustrates the historical devel-
opment of the urban landscape,
which Mr. Jellicoe wishes to
restore to the place it held in
the 18th century when town and
country were brought together
in the Bloomsbury squares.

We shall not find the answer
to the motor-car problem by
hacking the city to pieces to
make way for it in unlimited
numbers.

We must begin by designing
for people, by setting our archi-
tects and their professional col-
leagues to work to design a new
kind of town in which we can
live civilised lives, using the
motor-car without being en-
slaved by it.

If “Motopia,” which is richly

lors or the long-suffering victims
of the rush-hour out of their
while.

BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE.
JS 18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.
Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 12 houraw later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out.
entirely automatically.

bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
cooled down, and painted.

In their journey through the plant, the

aries of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
rris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
at corrosion and paint flaking.

"We came down, saw it, and bought it," she said.

The Maxwells had two children, a son and a daughter, but they were grown up.

CHILDREN with flaming torches led a march
        of 2,000 homeless last night—a march
        which ended with a bishop describing the
        plight as "a disgrace to the nation."

        Among the women in the quarter-mile long proces-
        sion which wound slowly from St. Paul's Cathedral to
        Southwark were mothers with babies in their arms
        with toddlers in push-
        chairs.
        At the end of the "croco-
        dile," men bore a huge
        banner which said simply:
        "No room in the inn."
        The two bishops who organ-
        ised the march—Dr. Robert
        Stopford, Bishop of London, and
        Dr. Mervyn Stockwood, Bishop
        of Southwark—took part in it.
        And from his pulpit at South-
        wark Cathedral, hard-hitting
        Dr. Stockwood spoke passion-
        ately about the problem of Lon-
        don's homeless—an emergency,
        he said, as great as the war.
        The cathedral, which holds
        about 1,200 people, was
        packed, and Dr. Stockwood's
        words were relayed by loud-
        speakers to hundreds who
        stood outside in the gather-
        ing darkness.
        The bishop said there were
        80,000 families in London wait-
        ing for homes—families living
        in overcrowded rooms, with
        inadequate facilities and shock-
        ing sleeping accommodation.
        REMEDIES
        And he suggested these reme-
        dies:
        A national housing authority,
        of which housing is now
        by the Government.
        • Priorities based on need,
        and if it is used for offices and
        factory building, it cannot be
        building homes," he said.
        • Control of land. "Is it right
        to leave speculators to deter-
        mine its value?" he asked.
        • In times of war the Govern-
        ment assumes control. Isn't the
        present emergency as grave?
        Among his other suggestions
        were mobile homes in London
        parks and open spaces, and the
        requisitioning of empty houses.

        DESPERATE
        As the bishop finished his ser-
        mon, 28-year-old Mrs. Gwyneth
        Cleaver, mother of two children
        who is living in an LCC centre
        apart from her husband, said:
        "This is our last desper-
        ate hope—that this march
        will move someone's con-
        science. Christmas isn't
        going to be much fun for us."
        Later, Dr. Stockwood, said: "I
        don't want to make this an anti-
        landlord thing. It's a question of
        human cupidity. We're all guilty
        of that—all ready to make a bit
        of money where we can.
        "What really sticks in my gul-
        let is the fact that a single room
        in, say, Hampstead, without
        facilities—water or anything—
        can be offered for £5 a week to
        desperate people.
        "And they are forced to take
        these rooms. They live in war-
        ren-six rooms, and maybe 30
        people in them. It's scandalous."

Picture by ARTHUR STEEL

WILLIAM RIPLEY was
formerly an assistant
in the barrel manu-
facture shop, but he
now works with his
father, James Ripley,
and Fred the Eker, in
the brewery. He is seen
on the way to the "Barrel
Monks" at the Churchills.

BY LESLIE DOWD

William Ripley
inherited his job from
his grandfather, who was an
assistant at Churchills.
There are few of us
who can say that we are in
the direct line of descent
from men who held the
same job 500 years ago, but
William Ripley, of
Churchills, can.

only a monk's bad temper
and a nasty disposition
could save him from being
locked in the barrel.
But it didn't happen for the
next 12 hours - not until
after his prayers and his
blessings from the Prior
had been said in the
Churchill Brewery - where
the traditional Barrel
Monks ceremony was to
take place one last time -
before the 500-year-old
custom was to be banished
for ever.
This last ceremony was to
take place on Christmas
Day.

THE LAST

The tradition began when
the monks of Churchill
Abbey produced the beer for
the village and for the
abbey itself and, with it,
the brewery became one of
the most important of the
abbey's many assets.
The abbot of Churchill Abbey
decided that the best way
to see the brewery kept in
order was to appoint a
"Barrel Monk" - a monk who
was responsible for
inspecting the beer barrels
to see that they were kept
in good condition and that
they were filled in the
proper way.
At Christmas Day, the
Barrel Monk had to drink
a barrel of beer in front
of the whole village - and
if he was unable to finish
it, he was locked in the
barrel for 12 hours.
This was not always a bad
thing, as the monks could
get very lonely, and after
a night's drinking it was
not too hard for them to
fall asleep for 12 hours.
But there were also some
monks who just could not
take the taste of the beer
and the barrels could be
very draughty, and William
Ripley's grandfather told
him that he had heard of
monks being half-frozen
when he had to stay in the
barrel overnight.

TRADITION

At a Christmas Day meeting
the monks elected the man
who was to be the Barrel
Monk for the next year. It
was a much sought after
job - not because of the
drinking - but because it
meant that the Barrel Monk
was not allowed to talk to
anyone for 12 hours of the
day in the brewery and had
to live a quiet life, so he
could concentrate on his
prayers.
But the job is being done
away with as the brewery is
being taken over by a new
owner from Sheffield, who
is bringing modern methods
and equipment. He will also
be bringing new beer. And
the monks are very upset.
They have petitioned their
Bishop and he has been in
communication with the
owner to try and preserve
the ancient custom - but
to no avail.

HE CLAIMED THAT THE NEW TOWN WAS BEING BUILT WITHOUT SUFFICIENT INDUSTRY TO MEET THE NEEDS OF THE GROWING POPULATION AND THAT THE RESULT WAS THAT OVER 40 PER CENT OF THE WORKING POPULATION WAS UNEMPLOYED.

MR. AMBROSE WAS SPEARHEADING THE SIT-IN AND WAS CALLING FOR AN END TO THE HIGH RATE OF UNEMPLOYMENT. HE SAID: "WE ARE NOT ASKED FOR HANDOUTS. WE ARE ASKING FOR THE OPPORTUNITY TO WORK AND TO CONTRIBUTE TO THE NATION'S PROSPERITY." THE SIT-IN CONTINUED ALL DAY WITH THE MEN TAKING TURNS TO KEEP A CONSTANT VIGIL AT THE MINISTRY'S OFFICES.

CAERNARVON, WALES : A GENERAL VIEW OF THE MASS MEETING

JONES, CHAIRMAN OF THE NANTLLE VALLEY UNEMPLOYMENT PEOPLES
COMMITTEE, WHILST HE IS HOLDING HIS DAUGHTER, 4-YEAR-OLD
NERYS IN HIS ARMS. HUNDREDS OF UNEMPLOYED FORMED A PROTEST
MARCH FROM THE VILLAGE OF PEN-Y-GROES, IN THE NANTLLE VALLEY,
TO ATTEND THE MEETING TO PRESS FOR THE EARLY ESTABLISHMENT OF
INDUSTRIES IN SOUTH-WEST WALES WHICH HAVE BEEN PROMISED TO

RISEN FROM 3,500 IN OCTOBER TO 6,000 IN NOVEMBER AND IS

PUT TO HIM THE URGENCY OF THE CASE FOR FINDING MORE WORK FOR
SOUTH-WEST WALES. THE DECISION OF RICHARD THOMAS AND BALDWINS

CHILDREN with flaming torches led a march which ended with a bishop describing their plight as "a disgrace to the nation."
About 2,000 homeless men, women and children from hostels and lodging houses streamed into St. Paul's Cathedral where a solemn requiem Mass was said before an altar arrayed with loaves and fishes.

As the rest of the congre-gation filed out, a large group of men, women and children remained to seek shelter for the night.
But just before 10 p.m. the Dean, the Very Rev. M. C. Hodson, decided the church was too crowded. He called in police to clear it.
The Dean, who is a member of the Government's Working Party on Homelessness, said he did not want to see anyone sleeping in the Cathedral.
"We must keep the Cathedral for services only," he told a journalist.
"I am afraid that it is not possible to allow people to sleep here."
Mr. A. E. M. Sanderson, national secretary of the LIM, which had organized the march, said 2,000 homeless had joined in.
"We wanted to draw public attention to the desperate plight of the homeless," he said.
"The march went off very peacefully. There was no trouble at all."

REMEDIES

ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â¢ There should be a two-year freeze on rents in London, and a freeze on the sale of empty houses.
ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â¢ London's three most power-ful councils should get together to find sites on which to build prefabricated housing.
ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â¢ A proportion of empty houses in the centre of London, now owned by the Church, should be converted into hostels for young people.

DESPERATE
The marchers left from the South London hostel of Dr. Donald Soper, who said: "This is not just a demo. It is a genuine march of desperate people."
Bishop of Woolwich, the Rt. Rev. David Sheppard, who joined the march at London Bridge, told the homeless people: "It is a disgrace to the nation that so many of you are sleeping rough or in dreadful accommodation.
"The Government should be ashamed that all of you have to live in these conditions. There are 25,000 homeless people in London. That is a national disgrace."
The Bishop said that young people from the provinces who came to London to look for work were finding it almost impossible to find a place to live.

CHILDREN with flaming torches led a march
of 2,000 homeless last night—a march
which ended with a bishop describing their
plight as “a disgrace to the nation.”
Among the women in the quarter-mile long proces-
sion which wound slowly from St. Paul's Cathedral to
Southwark were mothers with babies in their arms or
with toddlers in push-
chairs.

At the end of the "croco-
dile," men bore a huge
banner which said simply:
"No room at the inn . . ."
The two bishops who organ-
ised the march—Dr. Robert
Stopford, Bishop of London, and
Dr. Mervyn Stockwood, Bishop
of Southwark—took part in it
and from his pulpit at South-
wark Cathedral, hard-hitting
Dr. Stockwood spoke passion-
ately about the problem of Lon-
don's homeless—an emergency,
he said, as great as the war.
The cathedral, which holds
about 1,200 people, was
packed and Dr. Stockwood's
words were relayed by loud-
speakers to hundreds who
stood outside in the gather-
ing darkness.
The bishop said there were
80,000 families in London wait-
ing for homes—families living
in overcrowded rooms, with
inadequate facilities and shock-
ing sleeping accommodation.

REMEDIES
And he suggested these reme-
dies:
A national housing authority
with powers to borrow and lend
money at interest rates decided
by the Government.
Priorities based on need.
"If it is good for offices and
and if it is good for luxury
luxury buildings," he said,
control of land. "Is it right
to leave speculators to deter-
mine its value?" he asked.
"In times of war the Govern-
ment assumes control. Isn't the
present housing emergency as grave?"
Among his other suggestions
were mobile homes in London
parks and open spaces, and the
requisitioning of empty houses.

DESPERATE
As the bishop finished his ser-
mon, 28-year-old Mrs. Gwyneth
Cleaver, mother of ten children
who is living in an L.C.C. hostel
apart from her husband, said:
"This is our last desper-
ate hope—that this march
will move someone's con-
science. Christmas isn't
going to be much fun for us."
Later, Dr. Stockwood, said: "I
defy a man to make this an anti-
landlord thing. It's a question of
human cupidity. We're all guilty
of that—all ready to make a bit
of money where we can.
"What really sticks in my gul-
let is the fact that a single room
in, say, Hampstead, without
feeling, wallpaper or anything—
can be offered for £5 a week to
desperate people.
And they are forced to take
these rooms. They live in war-
rens—six rooms, and maybe 30
people in them. It's scandalous."

94-YEARS-OLD CRAFTSMAN.

Still working on a craft which has been in his family
since 1820 is 94-years-old Mr. Samuel Caldwell
of Canterbury (Kent), who is in charge of the stained
glass of the Cathedral, comprising thousands of square
feet of priceless glass, dating back to the 13th.
century. Twice in his lifetime, Mr. Caldwell
has removed the Cathedral's glass -once during the
1914-1918 war and again when the last war started.
Under Mr. Caldwell's supervision, the replacement of the
glass - a long and skilful process requiring endless
patience - has just been completed and he is now
at work designing and making stained glass to
replace the modern glass which was not removed and
was destroyed by bomb-blast. An authority on his
craft, with 77 years experience behind him, Mr.
Caldwell started work in Canterbury Cathedral when he
was 17.

old craftsman, seen at work in his Canterbury (Kent)
workshop, restoring a 13th. century medallion
representing "The last Supper". His health, sight
and hearing are all still exceptionally good.

A GIANT SHIP TO BE BUILT ON THE THULE WILL
BE LAUNCHED NEXT MONTH
JAMES
NOTE: The following is a Captains report regarding the 700 foot,
thirty-one-knot, FAST CARGO SHIP (YET TO BE
NAMED) THAT WILL HAUL THE FIRST CARGO OF
MERCHANDISE FROM GERMANY TO SOUTH AFRICA.

The report, submitted by Captain J.H. Hansen to the U.S. Maritime
Commission, reveals for the first time the revolutionary design
and construction of the ship which will make her the fastest
and most efficient freighter ever to fly the Allied flag. Hansen
credits the ship's designer, Lieutenant Commander W. E.
Hickling, with the development of a new hull design that
reduces drag by fifty percent. The ship's engines, which are
expected to develop 200,000 horsepower, will be capable of
driving the vessel at speeds exceeding thirty-one knots.
The ship's immense cargo capacity, which will be twenty
times that of the Queen Mary, will be loaded and unloaded
by a revolutionary automated cargo handling system. The
ship is expected to reduce by half the time required for
transporting goods across the Atlantic. The ship will be
launched from a special drydock in San Francisco on Tuesday,
March 14th. The U.S. Maritime Commission will hold a press
conference at the White House on Wednesday, March 15th, to
announce the ship's name and to provide further details
regarding its construction and operation. The first cargo
to be carried aboard the ship will be manufactured goods
from Germany, which will be shipped to South Africa.
The ship's official designation will be YUGOSLAVIA'S FINEST.
The ship, which is 700 feet in length, will have a beam of 110 feet and
a draft of 35 feet. It will be propelled by a single 300,000
horsepower turbine engine. The ship will be capable of
carrying 50,000 tons of cargo. The ship will have a crew
of 500 men. The ship will be equipped with the latest
navigational aids and safety equipment. The ship will be
armed with two 8-inch guns and a number of smaller
armament. The ship will be able to carry a complement
of 200 aircraft. The ship will be able to launch and
recover aircraft while underway. The ship will be able to
carry a complement of 500 troops. The ship will be able to
transport 2,000 passengers. The ship will be able to travel
at a speed of 31 knots. The ship will have a range of
10,000 nautical miles. The ship will be built at a cost
of $50,000,000.

cleanliness, men and women laboratory
workers are producing vaccines to combat

Meeting at Town Hall. 10.30 a.m.

The purpose of this meeting was to discuss problems facing the Coal Board in the North-Western division of Great Britain. The delegates included representatives from all the major coal producing areas, as well as members of the National Coal Board itself. The meeting was addressed by Lord Hyndley, the chairman of the National Coal Board, who spoke about the need for increased coal production and the importance of improving the efficiency of the industry. Other speakers included Mr. F. H. Haydn, the secretary of the Ministry of Fuel and Power, and Professor D. T. Davies, the director of the Manchester University Coal Research Unit. The delegates discussed a number of issues, including the need for investment in new mining equipment, the importance of training new miners, and the need for improved working conditions in the mines. The meeting concluded with a vote of confidence in the National Coal Board and a commitment to work together to ensure the future success of the coal industry.

30th MAY 1950
DEATH OF THE FIFTH VICTIM IN EAST LONDON FLATS COLLAPSE
FIFTH VICTIM FOUND IN RUINS
FIVE DEAD
EAST LONDON, MAY 30th. The death toll in the East London Flats Collapses at Canting Town, today rose to five when the body of the fifth victim was recovered from the ruins this afternoon. The building, which was erected last year, collapsed this morning. Mr. J. L. MEEK, Minister of Works, M.P., AND MR. J. EDWARDS, parliamentary secretary for Housing were present at the site this afternoon, and were briefed by the engineers on the collapse. MR. MEEK said that the Government would investigate fully into the collapse of the flats at Canting Town.
THE VICTIMS IDENTIFIED
THE VICTIMS OF THE COLLAPSE AT CANTING TOWN TODAY WHICH CLAIMS FIVE LIVES HAS NOW BEEN IDENTIFIED AS MR. A. BAKER AND HIS WIFE, MR. C. GRIMSHAW AND HIS WIFE AND A BOY, ROY GRIMSHAW. THE FLATS WERE ERECTED LAST YEAR AT A COST OF Ã‚Â£250,000 AND WERE SPECULATED AS BEING THE LAST WORD IN MODERN LIVING BY SIR ALAN COMRIE, THE ARCHITECT.
OFFICIALS INSPECT RUINS
MR. J. L. MEEK, Minister of Works, M.P., AND MR. J. EDWARDS, parliamentary Secretary for Housing, inspected the ruins this afternoon. They were informed by SIR ALAN COMRIE, the architect, that the collapse was due to the faulty construction of the blocks of flats.
THE NEW BLOCKS OF FLATS AT CANTING TOWN ARE TO BE PULLED DOWN AND REBUILT BY THE MINISTRY OF WORKS.
THE CITY OF LONDON WILL BE SHOCK BY THIS DISASTER.

Housing.. Slums

                                    A HOUSING COMMITTEE chairman has
                                    been officially told that a house owned
                                    by the company he controls is "unfit for
                                    human habitation."

                                    Yet he has so far refused to carry out
                                    the necessary repairs, at a cost of about
                                    £700.
                                    The seven-roomed detached house in
                                    Mount Pleasant, South Ruislip, Middlesex,
                                    is occupied only by 72-year-old Mr. Jacob
                                    James Harris, at a controlled rent of
                                    £2 0s 3d a week.
                                    His landlords are H. W. Cutler Property
                                    and Development Co. Ltd., of which 54-
                                    year-old Mr. Horace W. Cutler is a
                                    director. He is also chairman of the
                                    Conservative-controlled Greater London
                                    Council's Housing Committee, Britain's
                                    biggest landlord.

                                    No. 21, Mount Pleasant, is damp, shabby
                                    and neglected. Roof tiles are missing, gut-
                                    ters are rotting, paint is peeling. Hilling-
                                    don Council ordered the landlords to make
                                    it fit for human habitation by November
                                    23, 1967.
                                    "I could, of course, afford to carry out
                                    the work," bearded Mr. Cutler told me last
                                    week at his office in High Street, Pinner,
                                    Middlesex. "And I may yet do so.
                                    "But all over the country thousands of
                                                                        houses are falling into
                                                                        decay because of the
                                                                        stupidity of the Rent Acts,
                                                                        and that is my point."
                                                                        Mr. Cutler's refusal to
                                                                        carry out repairs is being
                                                                        made in protest against the
                                                                        Rent Acts which, he says,
                                                                        force landlords to spend
                                                                        large sums on repairs with-
                                                                        out any hope of return
                                                                        where rents are controlled
                                                                        and tenants are protected
                                                                        from eviction.

                                                                        'Too large'

                                                                        "Another tragic result of our
                                                                        present laws is underoccupation.
                                                                        It is ridiculous for a house of
                                                                        this size to be occupied by only
                                                                        one man.
                                                                        "Mr. Harris uses only the
                                                                        kitchen and one bedroom. The
                                                                        house is now far too large for
                                                                        Mr. Harris. He should be re-
                                                                        housed by the council."
                                                                        Mr. Cutler, a former mayor
                                                                        of Harrow, said he sympathised
                                                                        with Mr. Harris, who suffers
                                                                        from pneumoconiosis and whose
                                                                        only income is a £4 10s. a week
                                                                        pension.
                                                                        "With this chest trouble I
                                                                        cannot stand the cold," Mr.
                                                                        Harris said. "The house is
                                                                         chilly and damp. I keep wait-
                                                                        ing for the house to be put
                                                                        right."
                                                                        Mr. Harris moved into the
                                                                        house in 1940. Since his wife
                                                                        died several years ago he has
                                                                        lived there alone.
                                                                        Last year Mr. Harris was
                                                                        offered a place in an old
                                                                        people's home run by the
                                                                        council. "He refused it,"
                                                                        said Alderman A. J. Beasley, of
                                                                        Hillingdon Council, "as he is
                                                                        perfectly entitled to do."

1983-5236/44331

A THOUSAND policemen last night fought a vicious
pitched battle with a screaming 2,000 - strong mob
trying to storm St. Pancras Town Hall. It was violence
such as London has not seen since the hunger marches
of the 'thirties.

Time and again, lines of 50 constables, waving truncheons, charged
the solid mass of people. Women and children fell to the ground whimper-
ing hysterically. The roads around the town hall were like a battlefield.
And above the screams and shouts was heard the clang of ambulance bells.

Some people said that, after day-long taunts,
abuse and violence against the police, some of the
constables suddenly cracked.

Early today the hospitals were totting up the
casualty list. At least 14 people were injured, in-
cluding six policemen. Sixteen men and a youth
were arrested.

The fantastic, frightening scene flared after demon-
strators outside the two rebel blocks of council flats-
Silverdale House and Kennistoun House-joined forces
and marched on the town hall in a massive, anti-rent
increase protest.

A council committee meeting was hurriedly aban-
doned and hundreds of police reinforcements were
rushed in.

There were roars of anger
when the procession found
themselves facing a
three-deep line of police in
front of the town hall.

Down a half-dozen side-streets
squads of 50 to 100 policemen
were waiting in reserve.

The marchers fell back for a
few seconds, surprised at the
sight of so many police.

Then from the rows behind
the leaders came cries of "For-
ward, forward!"

Thus started a headlong on-
slaught by about 200 of the
young men among the marchers
against the centre of the long
line of police.

An inspector standing on a
bus yelled to the men:
"Stand fast lads, stand
fast."

The last of a group of
demonstrators perched
on a window-sill over-
looking the battle of St.
Pancras is dislodged,
protesting loudly. It is a
woman in slacks. Police
reach out as she drops,
then turn to continue the
struggle.

Chin in hand, Mr. Bressington (centre) taking it easy yesterday
AGAINST his nature
Trevor Bressington be-came one of Lord Robens' absentees yesterday.

Instead of going down the 880 yards into Cwm Colliery, near Pontypridd, South Wales, he was asleep in bed.

After 42 years in the pits he has dust on his chest, and a pain across his back which he thinks may be a slipped disc or a chill on his kidneys.

By staying at home in Beddau he joined the 40 per cent. of the coalface workers who failed to arrive for work at Cwm Colliery.

Everyone, except the Coal Board takes the absentee situa-tion philosophically.

SCRAPHEAP

Mr. Bressington, at 56, is still a good worker. He is a member of the pit consultative com-mittee, an apprentice training officer, and he does not like to miss a day's work.

But he—and many others of his age—are finding one thing.
BY JOHN DODD

£10 10s. a week. It is too big a drop from the £19 I get for five shifts at the coal-face.”

In his 42 years down the mines he has lost three close friends in accidents, and nearly died in one himself.

Yesterday, when he should have been working, he sat in a club with other miners, drinking pints and telling stories. Why
weren't the others working? One woke up late, two were on holiday, and two more were suffering from “bumps” and were off sick.

Today Mr. Bressington will be back at work. “Back with the 'donkeys' and the machines.”

Last week Lord Robens, the Coal Board chairman, con-demned absenteeism in the pits as a “national malaise.” He said that voluntary absen-teeism cost the Board the equivalent of 27,000 men's work last year.
They cannot keep up the pace. His union secretary, Mr. Bryn Williams, says: “In the old days a man was on the scrap heap at 45 but he could do his work at his own pace. Now he is expected to keep up with a machine until he is 65.

“They took the horses out of the pits and left the donkeys.” The “donkeys” at Cwm are men—numbering 1,400. Accord-ing to Mr. Williams more than 100 wear belts to support slipped discs in their backs, and 400 are suffering from dust, ranging from 10 to 60 per cent. dis-ability.

EXCUSE

He would rather smother his grandchildren than let them go down the pit.

Mr. Bressington says there are several reasons why men don't go to work on Mondays.

Some have to get up at 4.30 am. to travel 10 miles to the pit; some are fed up with chang-ing jobs down the pit. Others, like him, are feeling the pace of trying to keep up with machines.

And there are those who, if they miss a shift, earn as much from the sickness and compen-sation benefits. He says the best excuse is an accident down the pit.

WORST

Cwm Colliery's absentee figures are among the worst in South Wales. Yesterday 27.8 per cent. of the overall staff failed to turn up, something like 400 out of 1,400.

Production at the colliery averages 26 cwt. per man-shift, compared with a national aver-age of 34. The geographical conditions are partly to blame.

PRESS INFORMATION
FROM REINFORCED PLASTICS LIMITED

REINFORCED PLASTICS LIMITED DEVELOP 3,000 GALLON
UNDERGROUND PETROL STORAGE TANK FOR ES SO

In recent years the larger oil companies have been seeking ways
of increasing safety and cutting storage costs for petroleum spirit.
One of the major elements in the storage costs is the tank itself, and
also its concrete assessment.

Working to a specification from Esso Petroleum Company Limited,
Reinforced Plastics Limited have developed a 3,000 gallon, glass
reinforced plastic, underground storage tank measuring 7ft. in Diameter,
by 13ft. long, constructed entirely of Douglas glass fibres and Artite
polyester resin. The glass reinforced plastic construction of this
tank shows considerable advantages over other forms of storage tanks.
It resists bacterial and soil attack and will neither corrode nor leak.
It has a low installation cost, and because of its comparative light
weight, savings are made both in transportation and handling charges.

Tests have been carried out by Esso Petroleum and the Butterstan
College of Technology with the tank above-ground in a testing frame, and
buried in the ground to simulate all loadings to which the tank would be
subjected in service. The results show that the tank would be satisfactory
when installed in a single excavation, and butt-filled. In normal practice
where a tank is installed under the Forecourt of a service station it is
protected by a 9-inch re-inforced concrete slab. To test the effect of
normal vehicle loadings the road slab was deliberately made weaker, and
the tank successfully withstood the observed stresses.

These tanks can be made in sizes from 2,000 to 5,000 gallons
capacity, and in single and multiple compartment versions.

CAUTION: Technicians at the REINFORCED Plastics Limited, Cooberley,
Surrey, factory assembling a 3,000 gallon glass reinforced plastic
storage tank. This are recently undergone extensive testing by the Esso
Petroleum Company Limited, and the Butterton College of Technology.

23rd August, 1965

INDIA'S GREATEST RAILWAY TERMINI TRANSFORMED INTO
CAMPING GROUND FOR 6,000 MUSLIMS
18.10.47

India's greatest railway termini, Victoria Terminus
and Bombay Central in Bombay, have been transformed
overnight into camping grounds for 6,000 Muslims as
the sweeping tides of displaced minority peoples glow
in terror between India and Pakistan.
Eight men have died, children have been born and life's
entire meaning is compressed into an existence on bare
platforms and in open station enclosures between train
arrivals and departures.
They are all India Government, rail, postal, telegraphic,
income tax and customs workers, who on being given the
choice, expressed preference to work in Pakistan and are
being moved from inland Indian points to that capital
through this port.
The shift is being made by sea, but so heavy is the
rush that thousands have been inokloosed at the point of
embarkation, and have made their detraining stop their
temporary homes. Their descent on the two termini and the
natural demands have entirely dislocated sanitation and
hygiene in hitherto model and gigantic depots.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- Some of the 6,000 Muslims who have
made India's greatest railway termini,
Victoria Terminus and Bombay Central their
temporary homes while enroute to their new
homes in Pakistan. Their descent on the two termini
and their natural demands have entirely dislocated
sanitation and hygiene in hitherto model and
gigantic depots. Eight men have died and children
have been born while thousands of people have been
crowded into primitive quarters like these. Screens
of clothing can be seen strung up to shelter the
usually screened and secluded Muslim women from a
traveller's wondering gaze.

THE WORLD'S OUR MARKET FOR CARPETS.
18.3.46.
The famous Royal Wilton Carpet Factory was founded in the
17th century near Salisbury in a district noted for its
weaving since Elizabethan days. The factory received its
Royal Charter from William of Orange in 1701 and shortly
after, two Frenchmen, Anthony Dufessy and Peter Jemavie,
were said to have been smuggled over from France in
barrels to take charge of the factory. These Continental
weavers were masters of their trade, and the smuggling of
them was necessary owing to the strict laws of France
against craftsmen taking away the secrets of their trades
to foreign countries.
Hand-made carpets have been made at Wilton for many
important buildings in this country and throughout the
world, and now that the factory is released from war work,
it is busy on order from the United States, Canada and
South America etc. This picture taken recently at the
factory shows
Girls putting the finishing touches to handmade carpets
at the factory. They are for export.

THE BAD SADDLE?

One would think that 30-year-old Keneth Howard,
a saddler and harness maker of Freslingham,
Suffolk, would be pleased with life. He has just
commenced three months' leave from the Army. But
to Keneth this three months' leave means work! From
7 in the morning until 9 at night. This work is the
accumulation of 9 months' horses collars, harness
pads, bridles, binder canvasses, the property of
local farmers. They are all waiting for his expert
hands to repair them, ready for the busy time
ahead.

Nine months ago Keneth Howard ended another such
3 months leave as he did in 1941. Farming equipment
is even more important today than it was then.
The Suffolk War Agricultural Committee were responsible
for obtaining Keneth his leave, but the 3 months
granted is not sufficient time for Keneth to get
through the work owing to the fact that new harness
is almost non existent and the harness now in use
is in poor condition. By the time Keneth gets
through with them his 2 months is up, leaving no
time to cope with the binder canvasses that will be
needed to gather the coming harvest.
What worries Keneth is the fact that 33 years ago
he enlisted as a soldier and up till now he has not
even seen an Army horse, let alone a set of harness!
The Howard's have been saddler and harness makers
since 1805 in and around Freslingham, as Keneth feels
he would be of more use if left to carry on. He
repaired at one time repaired 8 harness collars. These
went when the war came. His mother carried on the
business when his father died ten years ago. He is
now the sole worker.
He has a brother in the R.A.F. and two of his sisters
are nursing. His job in the Army is repairing
equipment.
C.F.G.L. Keneth Howard re-padding with rye straw
one of the many collars. These he also covers with
wool blanket cloth; a repair usually lasts two
years.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORLD IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS 18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, as rated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats or paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did not give complete-
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.

Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 1½ hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.

B.P. INSTALLS EXPERIMENTAL BUOY AT HOSE.
B.P. G. 11513 7th December 1961.
A new type of mooring buoy for use in the loading
and discharge of tankers inconditions where conventional
berthing cannot be used, is being tested by British
Petroleum in the Thames Estuary. The prototype,
designed to enable tankers to be moored at a single
point, is being installed at the Nore about five
miles from the Kent Refinery of B.P. The work of
laying the buoy is being carried out by the Port of
London Authority.

The new buoy, which wasbuilt at Harland's
& Wolff's yard at North Woolwich, hasbeen designed
to eliminate some of the disadvantages associated
with existing single point moorings where varying wave
and tidal conditions cause deterioration of hoses, hindering
the movement of the buoy. The pendants or anchor hawsers
are one chain of the new buoy are of
a fixed length and are connected to an anchor bay set
into the seabed and filled with mud, stones. The bay is also
held by ground tackles. The pendants are always in tension
which restricts the movement of the buoy at all states of
the tide.
The hoses from the buoy are bolted to pipes secured
to the anchor heel by employing this arrangement the flexib-
le hoses are kept as short as possible and are at all
times clear of the seabed, thus avoiding deterioration
and wear. The pendants are led through the buoy well within
its diameter to the anchorbow. Consequently it is not
possible for a vessels hull to foul. They should fit in
the port at changes of tide.
If the experiments prove to be successful the
buoy could be used in areas where it is not possible to
construct conventional berths and where there is
insufficient depth of water at existing berths a buoy
may be sited in deeper water to accommodate the larger
vessels.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS 18.7.49.

Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.

Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steal, greasy state, and emerge some 1½ hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.

Windows and doors caved in a

The firemen were fighting an
outbreak at the British Gener-
ators, Ltd., in the High-street,
when the flames spread to an
acetylene cylinder.
Sub-officer Jenkins carried the
cylinder up from the basement
into the factory yard. Thirty
seconds later it exploded.

Like a bomb
Mr. R. Robins, proprietor of the
Royal Standard Hotel, said: "The
explosion was terrific, like a
bomb."
Mr. F. H. Clements, proprietor
of the Red Lion, said: "The doors
of my Lotei 200 yards away were
blown open. The damage might
have been caused by a V2."
Hundreds of people rushed to
the works and watched as
stretcher-bearers brought out the
injured.
Frames were held up in a quarter-
mile line. One of them, which
had been emptied of its passengers
just before reaching the works,
was shattered by the explosion.
Late last night the 22 families in
damaged Waterfall Cottages were
patching their homes with wood
from the wreckage and shovelling
debris into the road.

Home gone
White-haired Mrs. L. Few
opened up her grocery shop to
supply them with new gas mantles
Caretakers of British Genera-
tors, Mr. Ron. Butler, aged 51, and
his wife, Jean, 41, who live in a
flat above the factory, lost their
home.
Next door, Mr. and Mrs. Robert
Courteen, of the Waterfall Laun-
dry, returned two hours after the
explosion to find their home and
furniture wrecked.
Leading fireman James Gibb,
who went through all the London
blitzes, found that his home in
Waterfall-road had "received as
good a blitzing as I have ever
seen."
Mrs. Louise Senior, aged 72, who
was ill in bed next door to the

186475-78 HUM
THE 'CROWNING GLORY' - AS SUPPLIED BY BRITAIN'S
HEALTH SCHEME.

London: A woman's crowning glory is her hair, so the
mere male is led to believe - but like other feminine
charms these days, it may be false, in part or in whole.
Britain's comprehensive Health Service aids and abets
the deception regarding hair, and teeth, but few would
deny the benefits it confers on both male and female.
Over eight thousand people have taken advantage of free
wigs obtained under the health scheme, and although the
number of women applying is not known, a considerable
number of the applicants are believed to be women who
have lost all or part of their 'crowning glory'.
Of the applicants some 2,600 have so far been supplied
with wigs. One well-known London firm of wig-makers,
who export a considerable number of wigs to the United
States each month, have had 1,500 National Health
Service customers up to date, against their monthly
average of 50 private customers.
The making of wigs is a complicated and skilled art,
needing clever fingers and a sharp eye, for when man
competes with nature, nature usually wins, and to make
a wig which will deceive at close quarters is more than
difficult.
Most of the hair used for wig-making is obtained from
Western Europe; Italy, France and Germany contributing
a great part. Prices of the hair varies according to
the quality and colour, and this price affects the
cost of the finished wig. The most expensive wig to
buy, owing to the difficulty of obtaining the hair, is
a white one, the price of which lies between 25 and 100
pounds.
PHOTO SHOWS: With skillful hands June Jackson and Iren
Kadd knot hair into wigs. Apart from wigs supplied by
the Health Scheme and wigs for private customers, wig-
makers do a lot of work for stage and films.

126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the 'Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I'
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort. The
143-feet cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent
cabin altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 foot.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 feet - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the hoight
over the rudder is 50 foot.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve, air-cooled
radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower for
take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 foot, an economical cruising speed
of 200 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles. Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 foot,
increasing as fuel is consumed.

Herald Reporter
BRISTOL, Thursday.
HARRY PHILLIPS, 58-
year-old bespectacled
boiler-maker, of Ebbs Vale,
and Monmouth County
Councillor, is a man with a
mission.

He took a gulp of strong
rough cider while haymaking on a
Welsh hill farm as a boy. He has
been searching for a smooth, sweet
cider.

"If only the right blend of
sweetness could be found it might
take the place of beer in all the
pubs in Monmouth," he says.

Shade too sharp

So today the Ebbs Vale boiler-
maker went to Bristol for the
annual cider-tasting day at the
Long Ashton Agricultural Re-
search station. With growers and
cider experts from all parts of the
country, he sniffed and sipped 34
glasses of sharp bitter-sweet and
sweet varieties.

Clearing his palate with a piece
of dry biscuit after each taste, Mr.
Phillips tried hard to find his
ideal, but his taste was too dis-
cerning.

Even those with fine sounding
names such as Foxwhelp, Chisel
Jersey, Dymock Red, and Pisley
Hangdown, brought the same com-
ment. "No, it's just a shade too
sharp. It's the tang I don't like."

Lot to tell

Shaking his head as he left, he
said, "I've a lot to tell our educa-
tion committee, but I don't think
I found the cider I have been look-
ing for."

Prof. Bertie T. P. Barker, past
director of the Institute, told the
experts of experiments to cure
"cider sickness," which ruins the
taste and aroma of sweet cider. It
is caused by a family of microbes
which experts have been trying to
isolate since 1907.

His tip to cider makers was:
"Hand as soon as possible with
a sharp cider with a high acid
content."

LONDON: Battersea Power Station, first modern
power station built in London and massive landmark
familiar to Continental travellers arriving at
Victoria Station, is getting a new look.......
another chimney. Towering above railway lines and
river, the chimney is rapidly stretching up to the
337 feet of its three fellows. The power station
consists of two parts. Construction of the second
part was held up by the war and post-war shortages.
The new chimney will complete this second section.
Combined capacity of the two sections will be
503,000 kilowatts.
Power Stations are often blamed for the killing smog
which grips London during the fog season. (the
City of London has decided to obtain statutory
powers to reduce smoke in the City) but Battersea
and other modern power stations can plead 'not guilty'.
The towering chimneys emit no smoke, only steam
and vapour, for they are fitted with gas washing
and grit arresting plant.

A BRIEF but very important aid to British export trade is
being given by about six million silk worms which are being
reared at Lullingstone Castle Silk Farm, run by COM. LAIRDLAN MACDONALD, near Tonbridge, Kent. The ai and object of the
farm, which is now getting going again after the war, is to
develop and assist production of raw silk in this country, the
Dominions, and the Colonies, and what started off as a girl's
hobby, developed on a business footing in 1929, is now a
flourishing industry housed in one of Britain's ancient homes.

millions of them have been exported, and it was from their silk
that the Coronation robes for the Queen and the Princesses
were made. One of the difficulties at present being ex-
perienced is the lack of mulberry leaves on which to feed
the worms, for the eighteen acre plantations at Lullingstone
is only producing about half the number of leaves required
to feed six million tiny mouths.

weapon for spinning and weaving was first known in China at
least 3,000 years B.C. It was James I who endeavoured to
encourage silk worm rearing in this country by ordering the
importation and planting of thousands of mulberry trees, but
the Royal scheme was a failure. George 7 then took a keen
interest in the silk industry and in 1718 he granted a

A "RUSH" OF BUSINESS.

MJH/S. 28.

An enterprise which is enjoying the success it
well deserves is that begun by Mrs. N.E. Franklyn
of Salisbury. Four years ago, Mrs. Franklyn had
an hour's lesson from an old man in London, who
taught her the rudiments of the art of rush weaving.
He was highly skilled, but in the time available could
only pass on a fraction of his knowledge to Mrs. Franklyn.
However, with the little she had learnt, Mrs. Franklyn
with great determination, carried on to teach herself
this ancient craft, which goes back to the time when
rushes were spread on the floor for carpeting. Then
without any capital she took a little shop in East Street
(Salisbury) where she produced such articles as waste
paper baskets, table mats, seats for chairs and stools,
baskets for `ogs, dogs, fruit etc. etc. all made from
plaited rushes. These proved so popular that her business
steadily grew until today she employs a staff of four
and is looking for larger premises. Mrs. Franklyn collects
the rushes herself, from the rivers of Dorset and elsewhere,
and she has had many ducklings when rowing or wading to
harvest them. After the rushes have been cut, they have
to be dried out before being stored for subsequent use
and must be very carefully handled to prevent damage.
As far as can be ascertained, it is believed that there are
only two other businesses like Mrs. Franklyn's in the
whole country.

the ancient craft of rush weaving at her premises in

STRANDED EX-CONVICTS FIND A HOME IN A CHURCH
A NEW USE FOR EMPTY PEWS IN KENSINGTON

In the Royal Borough of Kensington there is a church where
every night stranded ex-prisoners and other unfortunate wrecks
of humanity find a place to sleep and call their temporary home.
In the gallery over the pews, and with a view of the altar and
the organ, they roll out their mattresses and get a peaceful
night's sleep, their washing strung out on a line from side to
side of this unusual place of worship. Theirstomachs are well
filled with sausage and mash cooked by one of their number in
the church kitchen. No charge is ever made for all this, and
many of them are enabled by thus having an "address" to get
public assistance and then employment - so difficult for a
man with nowhere to go when he leaves his prison after paying
society's price, or for those other men who have fallen on
hard times and for whom the Welfare State doesn't cater.
The Rev. Bertram Peake - known in the war as "The Tin Hat
Pastor"-who refused all honours for his work among the blitzed
Londoners,- has found this new use for his old church a
satisfactory continuation of his good, although to some minds,
unorthodox, work of caring for men's bodies as well as souls.
No man is refused at Golborne Church. No charge is made.
Men stay there on average six six weeks. For many hope and faith
are renewed, and jobs found before they move on. But there are
always more who come to take their place in the gallery of
comfort in this Kensington Church.

She learned the art at the
tender age of nine weeks
when most pullets are fully
occupied with the business of
pecking an existence.
And her teachers? A couple
of brown, rather aloof ducks,
her best friends.
The swimming chicken's
story is a success story. When
she arrived at Four Winds
Farm in the little village of
Chedburgh, near Bury St.
Edmunds, Suffolk, she was a
week-old outcast. All the
other 99 pullets pecked her.

when Mr. John Plummer, the
30-year-old farmer and his
pretty 24-year-old wife Ann,

and in no time she had taken

ming as effortlessly as—a
duck.

when she needs a rest from
swimming, up she goes on to
one of her friends' backs—a
down-covered raft.

feathers out, the ducks get to
work with their beaks with a
system that must feel like the

RADIO-CONTROLLED PLOUGH IS NEW HOPE FOR BRITISH FARMERS.

A radio-controlled farm tractor, developed by a British firm, (Tractors (London) Ltd.) in co-operation with the Automatic Control Section of the Royal Aeronautical Establishment is undergoing trials at recent, Hertfordshire.
Radio-control, normally used in the "power test", the target plane devised by anti-aircraft artillery practice, has been adapted for use in the tractor, which can be employed for ploughing and other farm operations.
Receiving radio signals operate sensitive electrical relays in the receiver, so that by means of compressed air servomotors the tractor can be made to run on a straight course, or to turn left or right. The plough can be raised when the tractor turns at the end of a furrow, the plough-raising system being cut out when other implements are attached to the tractor.
The radio-controlled tractor is so much lighter than the conventional type that fuel normally consumed in one hour is sufficient for a whole day's work.
P.s./p.e.--The radio-controlled tractor ploughing a field at Hareat, Hertfordshire, as farm dogs bark their annoyance at a strange contrivance which has no need of a ploughman.

A LOOK AT THE CITY OF THE FUTURE

Sea City - designed by a team of Britain's leading architects and engineers
as a logical 21st century successor to the present-day mainland city - was
unveiled today (February 20) at the London Hilton by the Minister of
Technology, Mr. Wedgwood Benn.

The imaginative concept, produced by the Pilkington Glass Age Development
Committee and designed by architect Hal Moggridge and engineers John Martin
and Ken Anthony, embraces a self-sufficient community of 30,000 living in
comfort and safety many miles out to sea.

The picture shows how Sea City would look from the air. Built on concrete
stilts and protected by a floating breakwater (seen in the foreground) and
by a curved 100 foot high city wall, it could be built in any of the shoal
waters that exist over 10 per cent of the surface of the ocean.

The majority of its inhabitants would live in attractively designed and
adequately serviced flats, as the picture shows. The floating islands
visible in the central lagoon, artificially heated by waste cooling water,
carry both public and private buildings providing the educational, social
and cultural facilities required by modern civilisation.

Outside the walls (right-foreground) special articulated container ships
berth in the "moat" of calm water to unload stores, while a hovercraft
heads for the harbour entrance to discharge its human cargo.
- end -

BUILDING UP OUR TIMBER STOCKS.

MJH/HT

During the two World Wars, our woodlands were
seriously denuded of timber. Today, the Forestry
Commission and private woodland owners are pressing
ahead with the vital task of forming new forests and
re-stocking the old. The year 1956 has marked a milestone
in the history of the Forestry Commission, for it has
seen the planting by the Commission of the one
millionth acre of new woodland. Thus the area of woodland
planted to date by the Commission is more than 1,500
square miles - an area larger than Kent, nearly
twice the extent of Glamorgan and nearly two-thirds
of Perthshire. This million acres is made up of some
500 forests, which are well distributed over the length
and breadth of Britain. In recent years, well over
100-million trees - including more than 10 million hardwoods -
have been planted annually by the Commission and many of
the forests are now producing timber in substantial
quantities; in 1955, the total production amounted to
600,000 tons. Today there is hardly a county without
a national forest and scenes such as these, in the
Commission's Rendlesham Forest in East Anglia, are typical
of what is to be seen in many other parts of the country.

GET OUT!
AFTER 60
YEARS IN
HER HOME

By Ken James
AN 80-year-old widow came
back from a seaside holi-
day at her son's expense to
the terraced house that has
been her home for 60 years.

Lying on the mat was a regi-
stered envelope containing the
Rent Act Form S—telling her
she must quit the house she
went to as a bride.

Last night white-haired Mrs.
Alice Thomas told me: "All I
want is to stay here until my
days come to an end. Yet they
mean to make me go."

The rent of the eight-roomed
house in Hatchard-road, Upper
Holloway—£11 18s. a quarter—is
paid partly by Mrs. Thomas'
married daughter, who lives up-
stairs.

No comment
But Mrs. Thomas pays the
rest and the £17 14s. 8d. a year
rates out of her only income, £2
a week pension. Rateable value
is £42—£2 over the maximum
under which a tenant is pro-
tected.

"If they'd only let me stay I'd
be willing to find a few more
shillings for a higher rent," she
said.

"I love my children very much.
But I'll sleep under an arch
sooner than live with them. I've
given myself blood pressure with
worry."

Hooper and Jackson, Padding-
ton estate agents who handle the
property, refused to comment
last night, or reveal the land-
lord's name.

With eight other tenants in
the road—the others have dif-
ferent landlords—old Mrs.
Thomas will be among the first
of the homeless in October, 1968.

THE GREAT JIB: STAR OF THE MACHINE AGE

Billed as "The Biggest Walking Drag-
line in the World, incorporating The
Great Jib", a machine that can certainly
qualify as one of the eight wonders of
the technical world made its debut at
Corby, Northants., today (Wednesday).
The machine, titled officially W.1400,
took Messrs. Ransomes & Rapier four
years to build on the site. It weighs
1,600 tons, has electric motors that
give over 3,000 motor horse power,
works for 20 hours a day, actually
walks -- with seven-foot steps -- and
is controlled by one man. Its purpose:
to remove strata covering the ironstone
bed down to a depth of one hundred feet.
Ironstone sells for a little over seven
shillings a ton; the W.1400 is designed
to uncover 400,000 tons of it each year.
For this reason, huge machine that it
is, it must "walk" over the area. After
settling in a spot, the machine swings
out with the great jib -- an arm 282
feet long, the tip of which is 175
feet above the ground. Then it drops a
22 ton scoop, lifts and drags away 27
tons of spoil. Within 60 seconds, the
scoop has emptied and is back, digging
in once more. PICTURE SHOWS: The biggest
walking drag-line (W.1400) in the world
seen here from the top of the great jib
at/its Corby (Northants.) site today.
