BATTLING FOR BRITAIN'S FORESTS.
168852 (DAW.) NEW GOVERNMENT RESEARCH STATION AIDS RECOVERY OF COUNTRY'S WOODLANDS.

FARNHAM, ENGLAND: At the Forestry Commission's new research station at Alice Holt Lodge, near this Surrey town, where
once the country's greatest struggles fought for the lives
of Allied war wounded, another type of "doctor" is battling
to save something more than Britain sacrificed in the war
effort. Degraded by urgent demands for timber during the
war, much of Britain's forest land has vanished, and what is
left is endangered by pest and disease, and here scientists
are battling to preserve Britain's woodlands.
Not only do they battle foresty pests - they actually
cultivate insects for export - certain insects are beneficial,
they prey upon parasites that infect trees.
The Research station at Alice Holt Lodge, an old mansion
standing in some 2,000 acres of former Crown woodlands, has
an extensive library, laboratories, photography, and pathology
sections.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The Entomologist uses a suction tube to
collect parasites from brooding cages, in which parasites
and their young have been cultivated.
Under normal conditions, harmful insects are kept in check
by natural enemies. This calls for the introduction of
parasites to control the new pests. Natural enemies of
harmful insects are insectivorous birds and mammals, and
a large variety of parasites and predatory insects which destroy
a large proportion of eggs, larvae and pupae.

31st March, 1948. 2.

war, much of Britain's forest land has vanished, and what is
left is endangered by pest and disease, and more scientists
are battling to preserve Britain's woodlands.
Not only do they battle forestry posts - they actually
cultivate some for export - certain insects are beneficial,
they prey upon parasites that infect trees.
The research station at Alice Holt Lodge, an old mansion
standing in some 2,000 acres of former Crown woodlands, has
an extensive library, laboratories, photography, and pathology
sections.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The Entomologist uses a suction tube to
collect parasites from brooding cages, in which parasites
and their enemies have been cultivated.
Under normal conditions, harmful insects are kept in check
by natural onomies. This calls for the introduction of
parasites to control the new pests. Natural enemies of
harmful insects are insectivorous birds and mammals, and a
large variety of parasites and predatory insects which destroy
a large proportion of eggs, larvae and pupae.

The English city of Nottingham, famed for its lace, is now
one of the key points in the battle against one of the
most irritating post-war shortages endured by Britain's
women - the lack of nylon stockings.

factories which before the war were turning out stockings
at the rate of nearly a million dozen each year.
Now, after long experiment, overhaul of machinery and
adjustment of plant to handle nylon yarn, they are

POST MORTEM BY DR. A. H. McKECHNIE, GOVERNMENT PATHOLOGIST, GIBRALTAR.

ON 24TH. JUNE 1926.

HISTORY.

The body of the above deceased Sergeant H. A. ROBERTS, R.A. F., was identified by Lieutenant W. G. BRIGHT, R.A.F., who stated that the deceased was found dead in the Officers' Mess, Gibraltar Aerodrome, on the morning of 23rd. June 1926. It is suspected that the deceased was poisoned by his wife, who according to Lieutenant BRIGHT, had been in the habit of administering poisons to her husband. There is no history of any acute illness.

AUTOPSY FINDINGS.

The body is that of a well-built man aged 30 years. Rigor mortis is well marked. There are no external marks of injury. The stomach contains about 8 ounces of partially digested food. The intestines are normal. The liver, kidneys and heart are healthy. There is no sign of any disease. There is no evidence of any injury or disease which could account for death.

In view of the suspicions expressed by Lieutenant BRIGHT, that the deceased had been poisoned by his wife, the organs of the body were preserved and sent to the Government Analyst for further examination for any toxic substances. This examination will be completed as soon as possible and the results will be reported on later.

No other cause of death is suspected.

Signed:-

A. H. McKECHNIE,

Government Pathologist,

Gibraltar.

LONDON'S LATEST POWER STATION.

JS 21.1.53
London's new power station, at Bankside, opposite
St. Paul's, has now begun to supply electricity.
In spite of great opposition by official bodies, the
decision to build this power-station opposite the
cathedral was pressed ahead. It has been designed by

completed, will comprise four 60,000 kw generating
sets in a steel-framed structure faced with bricks.
The main building is 840 ft. long, 240 ft. wide and
90 ft. high, and the single chimney is 300 ft. high.
Bankside is the first to be designed for oil burning,
and a river jetty has been built for oil tankers,

OLD CORNISH COPPER MINE YIELDS URANIUM ORE. MJH/P. 1.

Wheal Edward Mine, on the edge of the cliffs at St. Just,
three miles from Land's End, Cornwall, may have a new lease
of life as the result of the work now being carried out their
by new modern prospectors with geiger counters. For years
the mine was worked for copper in the hey-day of Cornish
mining, but the financial structure of the old mineral companies
made no provision for the time when underground exploration
was necessary or when thinner lodes were met and by 50 years
ago, most had closed, until today only two are working, both
for tin. Wheal Edward, however, attracted the attention of a
prospecting geologist, Mr. Richard Rumbold of Streatham (London)
who was surveying the whole of West Cornwall for radio-active
materials, combining this work with the field testing of modern
prospecting equipment. His geiger counter ticked encouragingly
when samples of ore were produced from the ancient mine and by
scrambling down the cliff edge, he found a fairly easy means
of access. Otherwise an elaborate winch gear would be needed to go
down the vertical main shaft, which disappear dramatically
into the dark ground. Now it is likely that a company will
be formed to re-open the old mine for uranium ore.

seen testing the native rock 120feet down the old heal Edward

No hope remains of saving

ings will go on. But Sir Andrew
added: "We must make sure

lives."
Heavy rain yesterday poured
into the crater left by the sub-
sidence that trapped 129 men
last Thursday. The water
caused two fresh subsidences.

through which teams had been
entering the mine. Rescue
workers were switched to the
task of improving drainage with
high-powered pumps (above).
Down the neighbouring Bank
Pit workings, through which 116
men were rescued during the
week-end, efforts to clear the
poisonous "black damp" gas
continued.
Mr. Philip Noel-Baker, Minis-
ter of Fuel, visited both pits
yesterday. News of the disaster
reached him in Greece and he
decided immediately to fly home.
Only two of the miners who
were saved are now in hospital.

BANKSIDE POWER STATION: PRODUCTION GETS UNDER WAY

London: An industrial project which has aroused much
controversy from the time of its conception has just gone
into operation. It is the Bankside Power Station, at
which the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator, of
about 80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed, on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the power station was so strong that in
January, 1947 a public inquiry was held, with the result
that the scheme has given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will comprise
four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the oil
consumption at full-load (10-hour day) being 67 tons
an hour, consuming in one winter's day about 850 tons.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The pump house at the river jetty which has
been built to accommodate tankers and barges. The oil will be
brought up the river mainly by self-propelled barges from
which it will be discharged by these pumps through a tunnel
to underground storage tanks at the rear of the power
station.

'DOORMAT' STRETCHER CAN AID MINE RESCUES
October 8th 1963 PAR 105646-1 (PNR/P-R)

'DOORMAT' STRETCHERS CAN AID MINE RESCUES

An old piece of colliery conveyor belt that
was once used as a doormat looks like
revolutionising mine rescue work in the
South Yorkshire coalfields, and may win a
National Coal Board Divisional award for
50-year-old JACK HUBY of Carcroft, near
Doncaster, fire and rescue officer at
Bullcroft Colliery, near Doncaster.
Jack started experimenting with the 3/8in.
thick belt four months ago and came up with
a new type of stretcher which he is seen here
(on right) demonstrating.
In a recent demonstration, miners saw Jack
dragged by an engine along a rough railway
track at 10 miles an hour. Then, still
strapped in the stretcher - which fits snugly
around the patient - he was pulled through
a 3ft.6in. water pipe.
Mr. Albert Wilds, the Bullcroft Colliery
manager, said: 'There's no doubt it is a
real step forward in mine rescue work.
This stretcher can be used extensively in
underground coal seams where rescue teams
find it impossible to take conventional
stretchers. It will get injured miners
up from the coal face quicker than any other
type.'
Cost of making the Huby Stretcher is
negligible.

Science Reporter
OUT of the silvery North Sea
yesterday shot a 40ft. fountain
of flame—high enough to kindle
the hopes of every money-minded
housewife in the land.

For behind that flame is gas.
Enough in a day to cook the dinners
and heat the sitting rooms of a
300,000 people.
And enough to allow British Petro-
leum, who have been drilling for gas
deep under the North Sea along with
7 other strike-hungry companies, to
announce cautiously: "We are
optimistic."

DIAMOND TIPPED

Yesterday was flare-test day on Sea
Gem, BP's 5,600-ton, 136ft.-high boring
rig, whose diamond-tipped drills first
struck a reserve of natural gas two
miles under the North Sea last
September.
Engineers who have been busily
constructing a well to draw up the
precious fuel, brought up their first
large "bucketful" to sample it for quality
and quantity.
Their announcement: excellent gas,
and enough of it to provide 10million
cubic feet a day, "a very encouraging
start."

SECOND DRILLING

This is enough to satisfy the needs
of a town the size of Nottingham. Or,
of course, 10 towns of 30,000 each.
I flew in a Heron plane, 200ft.
of the gaunt, black skeleton of Sea
Gem, 42 miles east of the Humber, and
the yellow spindle of flame burning off
the surplus gas as it emerged.
BP's North Sea project co-ordinator
Bob Holroyd said that a
second drilling would start
before the end of the year

Sea Gem.

promise, there will be a
third, and a fourth, and a
fifth. "Until, in fact, BP are

500million cubic feet of gas a

North Sea scheme a going

us cheaper prices, lower bills
every quarter.

FERRYBRIDGE . YORKSHIRE.
THREEX 350-ft. cooling towers
were blown down and a
huge oil rig was torn from its
moorings yesterday as gales of
up to 100 mph. swept Britain.

At least seven people were killed
and scores were injured.

In the cooling tower collapse at a
£70million power station, hundreds
of workers escaped—because they
were on a tea-break.

Last night another tower at the
power station in Ferrybridge, York-
shire, was in danger of collapsing.

FALLING CONCRETE

The station is due to come into
operation this year and is one of the
biggest in Europe. Only three men
were slightly hurt by falling concrete
as the towers crashed into rubble.
Damage is estimated at £2million.

But the luckiest men alive today
are the 30 workers aboard the
£21million oil rig Ocean Prince which
snapped a dozen steel hawsers at
Middlesbrough, Yorkshire, and
floated into the River Tees before
dawn yesterday.

Four times the men escaped death.

Escape No. 1 came when
the rig crashed into the side
of an oil tanker.

Escape No. 2 came a quarter
of a mile downstream when the
rig's crane sliced through two
power cables strung across the
river lighting up the sky with
huge flashes.

Escape No. 3 happened as the
rig bore down on a small dredger
in the river. Aboard the
dredger was 2,000lb. of gelignite
—but the dredger crew towed it
to safety and then took to their
boats to escape. Finally came:

Escape No. 4, when the oil rig
bit deep into a mudbank with-
in sight of the open sea and
almost capsized.

Last night, after the men had
been rescued by launches, the
River Tees was closed to ship-
ping with the oil rig blocking
the sea route. Tugs were stand-
ing by.

made to tow the rig back up
river, where she is being fitted
out before joining the North

THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION

As sailing fast gains popularity as a sport,
modern mass production methods derived from
those developed during the war for making
wooden aircraft are being applied to the
manufacture of boats at Hamble, Hampshire,
factory of Fairey Marine Ltd., a subsidiary of
the Fairey Aviation Company.
The craft are 'hot-moulded' from planks of
wooden veneer, a method which eliminates the
old and laborious method of boat-building by
individual craftsmen.
The shell of each boat is composed of layers
of planks applied to a mould to form 'skins'
glued together. Each shell is baked by
steam heat up to 100 degrees Centigrade for
about half an hour. Then it is taken out of
the oven and removed from the mould.
The resulting boat, it is said, will last a
lifetime and is proof against all the normal
ills which affect boats built by other methods.
More than 1,000 boats were produced at Hamble
in 1957, ranging from 7ft.6in. dinghies to the
26ft. Atalanta sailing cruiser.
Over one-third of the output is exported.

OIL-DIP FOR LONG STORAGE

A special process is now being used in the packing stations
of the Yorkshire Egg Producers Limited, Bridlington,
Yorkshire, to preserve eggs during storage. This process,
known as "egg dipping", has so far only been carried out on
a small scale in the U.K. although it is widely used in the
U.S.A., Canada, Denmark, Holland and Australia. In 1949, the
Food Ministry carried out large-scale trials of the process.

Deterioration of eggs is caused mainly by bacterial
infection through the shell and partly by the escape of
moisture and carbon dioxide, causing the albumen to break
down. The colourless, odourless and tasteless mineral oil,
in which the eggs are dipped before being placed in cold
storage, fills the pores of the shell and prevents microbial
invasion and greatly reduces the loss of moisture and carbon
dioxide. The Shell Crude recommended for this application is
Shell Ondina Oil 17.

The Yorkshire Egg Producers Ltd. handle approximately
1/25th of the total eggs packed in the U.K. (in 1953, this
represented nearly 200 million eggs). They possess 9 packing-
stations, at which eggs are sorted, "candled" to detect

OIL-DIPPING AIDS EGG STORAGE

A special process is now being used in the packing stations
of the Yorkshire Egg Producers Limited, Drighlington,
Yorkshire, to preserve eggs during storage. This process,
known as "egg dipping", has so far only been carried out on
a small scale in the U.K., although it is widely used in the
U.S.A., Canada, Denmark, Holland and Australia. In 1949, the
Food Ministry carried out large-scale trials of the process.

Deterioration of eggs is caused partly by bacterial
infection through the shell and partly by the escape of
moisture and carbon dioxide, causing the albumen to break
down. The odourless, colourless and tasteless mineral oil,
in which the eggs are dipped before being placed in cold
storage, fills the pores of the shell and prevents microbial
invasion and greatly reduces the loss of moisture and carbon
dioxide. The Shell grade recommended for this application is
Shell Ondina Oil 17.

The Yorkshire Egg Producers Ltd. handle approximately
1/19th of the total eggs packed in the U.K. (in 1953, this
represented nearly 200 million eggs). They possess 9 packing-
stations, at which eggs are sorted, "candled" to detect
interior flaws, graded by weight, stamped and repacked for
delivery to retailers.

Operated by 3 assistants, the oil-dipping machine can dip up to

PROVISIONAL APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE CHAIRMAN - 2001

Mr. R. M. "Bob" Perry was today provisionally appointed Chairman of the Republican National Committee by acting Committee Chairman, Ms. Mary Ellen Kilpatrick. This appointment will be effective immediately and is provisional pending official confirmation by the full Committee at its next scheduled meeting in September.

Mr. Perry, a businessman from Texas, replaces Mr. William "Bill" Harris who resigned from his post last week to pursue private business interests. Mr. Perry is a well-known figure in Republican circles and has served in various capacities within the party at both the state and national levels.

"I am honored by this provisional appointment and I look forward to working with the Committee to further the goals of the Republican Party," said Mr. Perry. "We have a lot of work ahead of us, and I am eager to get started."

Ms. Kilpatrick expressed her confidence in Mr. Perry's ability to lead the Committee during this transition period. "Bob Perry has the experience and the dedication to lead the Republican National Committee," said Ms. Kilpatrick. "I am confident that he will do an excellent job."

Further details regarding the committee's upcoming meeting and any other business will be announced at a later date.

Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole have

est coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge

17.3.40.
A new tunnel, driven under the river Thames from Battersea
Power Station to Chelsea, will carry cables between the power
station and a new sub-station in north-west London. The
2,800 ft tunnel - one of the most modern in the engineering feats
in London - takes 500-ft-radius bends to miss the piers
of the Victoria Railway Bridge, but in spite of this
it was only 2/8-inch out when it connected with the pit dug at
the Chelsea end. Continuous shifts working day and night
since in st September have averaged 80 feet per week, and
pressurised air is had to be used to keep the engineers going.
At one point the tunnel air pressure of 10lb per square inch
had to be increased to 30lb to stop the water from bursting
through. The internal diameter of the tunnel is eight feet
and it is being lined with 1,900 tons of cast-iron lining.
It is 76 feet below ground level on the south bank, and 28
feet under the river bed at the highest point.

NEW CREPE & RAYON INDUSTRY IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
A new industry which has sprung up in Northern
Ireland is the preparation and weaving of
rayon crepe and other rayon fabrics.
Crepe Weavers Ltd., of Newtownards, Co. Down,
which commenced in 1946 occupies part of Newtownards
Airport which was originally built for the production
of aircraft.
It employs 125 people at present but will employ 200
people by the end of the year when the mill is fully
equipped.
Owing to the male unemployment situation in the
district it is the intention of the firm to employ
60 per cent men and 40 per cent women.
The production target for the end of the year is 30,000
yards of Rayon fabrics per week, of which between 50
and 60% will be for export.
Most of the workers engaged are trainees formerly
agricultural labourers and laundry workers.
Care has been taken not to engage workers from linen
textile mills in the district which would have added
to the production of the new firm but would have
caused difficulties in the established firms.
OPS. One of the employees works on an improvised
fixture which operates the drawing in preparation of
the works for the looms.

machines for this purpose arrive.

Crane delivering concrete on the top floor

diagonally from the beam, works horizontally
from the main structure - pushing materials
not only to be lifted vertically, but served
horizontally across the building site to the
spot where the craftsmann needs them.
The number of bricklayers working on a site
can be doubled - with the extra men delivery
of bricks to them, with the aid of the new cranes,
which is used to remove excavator earth, unload
material from lorries, lifting floor joists and
window and door frames, roofing timbers and tiles,
and in general speed-up all building.

The following information, with regard to the rationing of petrol and oil for use in private motor cars, has been supplied by the Ministry of Transport. The national interest in the conservation of petrol and oil is recognised. Therefore, it is requested that all owners of private cars should, if possible, restrict the use of their vehicles to essential purposes only. MACE FOR BRITISH JEWELLERS' ASSOCIATION 26.1.55.

The British Jewellers' Association, which
represents nearly 2,000 manufacturing and
wholesale jewellers, has become a patron
of its own trade. The Central Council of the
Association recently decided that the ancient
art of silversmithing was in serious danger
of extinction without public support.It was
decided that the Association should commission
a special piece every year, thus building up its
own collection of fin silver-ware and, at the same
time, setting an example to similar organisations
who might become patrons to the trade. The first
piece,amodern silver mace for use upon ceremonial
occasions, has now been completed, designed by the
well-known designer R.H.Hill, and made by a london
firm of silversmith's.

I.N.P.PHOTO SHOWS:- A close-up of the 21 inch solid
silver mace, which employs the three
motifs of the sun, moon and mercury, which
figure in the Associations coat-of-arms.

A FARM WITH A DIFFERENCE.

A farm with a difference is that run by Mr. T. Donnellan
at Warsash, Southampton. For on his farm Mr. Donnellan
has no cows, horses, pigs or sheep - his "stock" consists
of crabs, lobsters, crawfish, prawns, oysters etc., for he
is a sea-food farmer. His "fields" are 4,000 sq. yards
of water where thousands of sea-animals caught by Hampshire
and Cornish fisherfolk are kept in salt-water storage ponds
for 30 days before being sent away to end up on a plate.
Mr. Donnellan's two daughters Catherine (9) and Mary (7)
love to help on this fascinating farm and are not the least
bit frightened of the crabs, lobsters etc. - on the contrary
they love them and can name all the 5,000 different species
and varieties of sea animals, worth £4,000 kept on the farm.
The little girls even wade in the ponds at low water in bare
feet and are X not the least afraid of getting their toes
nipped.

are seen helping their father MR. T. DONNELLAN, who is holding
a giant crawfish, to collect crabs, lobsters etc. for
despatch to various hotels, restaurants, etc. on their
farm at Warsash, Southampton. Mr. Donnellan also supplies
many ocean liners with fresh crabs, lobsters etc.

A young authoress who pushed her husband's sports car into the road to prevent it being damaged by high winds, saw him- self and the car narrowly miss being buried under a pile of bricks and rubble 20-ft. high.

A three-storey empty bombed house collapsed on to the road, but its high bricks had crashed right on to the car.

The owner of the car, Mr. Peter Broadhurst, of Leverett Manor, Her- tford, was in his car at the time, with his wife. He had bought the car only four days ago. "I just got out of the car," he said, "when the house collapsed and only by the mercy of God escaped myself and the car from under the debris."

Mrs. Maureen Johns, 27, authoress, was helping Mr. Broadhurst to push the car round to park. "I couldn't get the car round," she said, "and jumped out of the car as the whole house crashed behind."
She covered the whole scene with a blanket.

ings of 200 actual houses (not architect

Lorries unloading shale from Chislet Colliery, Kent, at Pegwell Bay
where it will be used in the construction of the new international

ROYAL PRESENT FOR KING OF THAILAND. 26.4.50.

For their wedding present to the King of Thailand,
their Majesties, have chosen a service of Worcester
Royal Porcelain. The pattern chosen is known as the
Royal Lily Pattern and is printed in underglaze blue
and enriched with gold. The design was originally adapt-
from the Chinese in the Worcester factory between 1757
and 1788, and was selected by King George. III and Queen
Charlotte when they. visited the works in 1788.
Throughout its 200 years history, the Worcester factory
has produced distinguished underglaze blues. The Worcester
factory was one of the first to be established in England
in the middle of the eighteenth century. European potters
were discovering how to produce porcelain similar to the
Chinese ware, and its early products rank with those of
Bow and Chelsea in the "Golden Age" of English porcelain.
The craftsmanship inherited from those days has helped
to produce this royal present.

Believed to be the only contest of its kind in the world,
the annual Hop Stringing Competition, organised by the
East Kent Hop Planters Association, took place
to-day at Spitsbrook, Collier Street, Kent. About 40

most of them coming from families which have worked in
the hop gardens for generations, took part. The
stringer's job is to prepare hop gardens for the next
crop by putting up a complicated pattern of strings which
the hops can climb. He works from with a pole 30 feet

competition, each stringer completes a "bay" of 800 -
900 hills. Some 40 miles of string are used in the process.

(XM) L.C.C.'S NEW PAINT-TESTING LABORATORY

In order to enable a systematic check to be maintained
on the qualities of the 200,000 gallons of paint used
annually by the London County Council the chemical
laboratories at County Hall, London, S.E., have been
extended and re-equipped at a cost of about £2,000.
The Public Health Department's Chemist-in-Chief has for
some years been responsible for testing paints used by
the Council on its housing estates, schools and other
establishments. The large quantities of paint now
needed and the increasing complexity of materials used
in manufacture have made it necessary to improve testing
facilities and to instal modern equipment for measuring
such qualities as weathering, hardness and anti-corrosion.
The new paint laboratory has been equipped to supplement
the examination of decorative and protective coatings
which has been made hitherto. The L.C.C. spends
considerably more than £1,000,000 each year in
its painting programme.

MORE FURNITURE GOES INTO ARMY HUTS DESPITE QUIT NOTICES.

A policy of 'sit tight' and await developments has been adopted
by ex Servicemen who, with their wives and children, have moved
into unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire, because they were unable to find other
accommodation as a result of the housing shortage. Notices to
quit have been served on some of the 'squatters', and German
prisoners have been brought in by the military authorities to
start pulling down huts on the site scheduled for demolition.

and their 3½-year-old daughter Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an
inspector in a Diesel factory, is a former Petty Officer in the
Navy who won the British Empire Medal for bringing a lifeboat
safely to land after it had been 39 days in the Atlantic following
the torpedoing of a troopship. Whilst recovering from his
ordeal in New York he met Caroline - now his wife - who comes
from Brooklyn.

THE PROGRESS OF A NEW TOWN
JS 16.8.50
HARLOW is one of eight New Towns designed for the reception of
population and industry from the crowded area of Inner London,
and which are expected to take about 250,000 Londoners. Harlow's
contribution to this will be an increase in population of

ROBOT MOTHERS: FIVE
Five robot mothers, built and
trained to rear babies, have been
produced by American scientists
and placed in experimental
homes. The aim is to learn
whether artificial mothers can
provide the emotional needs of
a child, as well as the physical.
The robots, operated by a
television set and a sound amplifier
can move, rock a baby, change
diapers, and sing lullabies. If
they are successful, they may
be available to the public in
10 to 15 years.

ROOM FOR 1-6
The robots, called "RoboMoms"
are equipped with a video screen
that shows the child a picture
or a story. They can also play
music, speak and even cry if
the child is crying. They have
been tested on babies aged 1 to 6
years old and have proved to be
quite successful. Researchers are
hopeful that the RoboMoms will
help alleviate the shortage of
childcare workers in the United
States. The project is funded by
the National Science Foundation.

Incoming radio signals operate sensitive electrical relays in the
receiver, so that by means of compressed air servomotors
the tractor can be made to run on a straight course, or to turn
left or right. The plough can be raised when the tractor
turns at the end of a furrow, the plough-raising system being
cut out when other implements are attached to the tractor.
The radio-controlled tractor is so much lighter than the
conventional type that fuel normally consumed in one hour is
sufficient for a whole day's work.

It has taken the Women's Land Army to find out
that Miss Littler, a volunteer in the employment
of the Flintshire War Agricultural Executive
Committee possesses the gift of water divining.
Miss Littler joined the Women's Land Army March 1941
and is one of 9 girls employed on gang work.
Recently they were working on a piece of land which
was constantly being flooded by a hidden spring.
Mr. J.T. Richards, the Executive Officer of the
Flintshire War Agricultural Executive Committee, had
made extensive efforts to have the spring located.
Finally, he asked the 9 members of the Women's Land
Army, who were clearing the land, to try with a
hazel stick to see if they could divine this spring.
Miss Littler was found to be the only one who
possesses this unusual gift. 1942-1950/6682
Since Flintshire farmers have heard of this there
have been many requests for her services, to help
in reclaiming flooded land and so save hundreds
of pounds in drainage. Also farmers wish to use
her to help to discover water for sinking wells.

is to cut a forked twig from a hazel tree.

The day the flats collapsed. June 18 1968
(Picture story : Pringle/Photocall).

MISS IVY HODGE, grey haired and marked
by the memory of Ronan Point flats disaster, was helped
into a packed Newman Town Hall yesterday (Tuesday)
to re-live those moments of horror.

"I went to bed at 10.45 - and read a little,"
said the 55-year-old woman, released especially from
Poplar Hospital to give evidence at the inquiry.
"At 2.25 I was awake and I went into the
kitchen to fill the kettle for a cup of tea ... I
can't remember any more. There was a flash across the
ceiling and then the ceiling began to flake."

The inquiry was hushed as Miss Hodge
who lived in a 19th floor flat at Ronan Point - and
is still alive - chose her words. Asked if she
smelt gas she replied : "I didn't smell any gas
and I have a good sense of smell."

She nodded at the end of giving evidence
and was helped back to hospital by two friends.
She is under treatment for burns to her
face arms and legs.

---ends---.

similar board turned to the reverse side, which has the

IN SOME WAYS Beaconsfield
Buildings, just a short bus ride
from the glitter of Piccadilly
Circus, could be considered a
showplace.

For to film producers at least, the
grey-bricked, five-storey blocks of flats
seem to have an irresistible fascina-
tion.

There was Max Bygraves in Cry From
the Streets, and Spare the Rod and
Spoil the Child. There was Joe Brown
in What a Crazy World. And Jess
Conrad in The Boys.
Each finding in the rows of miserable
flats—known without affection as The
Crumbles—the perfect setting for a film
about slums.

For today Beaconsfield Buildings has
about as much in common with the
affluent gadget world of 1964 as it did
when Prime Minister Disraeli laid the
foundation stone in 1875.

The plumbing is still Victorian. There
are few separate kitchens, few bath-
rooms, and landing lavatories shared by
between five and eight families.

On Sunday 200 of the 440 tenants
marched five miles from the flats in
Randall's Road, near King's Cross, to the
Chelsea home of Housing Minister Sir
Keith Joseph. To ask him to pull The
Crumbles down.

Their case? Well, it can be found in
the story of just three families.
CASE ONE: Mrs. Bridget Welsh, aged 45,
wife of a labourer, lives in three rooms
and a partitioned kitchen at £1 14s. 2d.
a week. Her flat is spotless.
She said: "Six weeks ago my girl
Geraldine—she's 10—caught dysentry.
Not from our lavatory because I clean it
constantly, and not from her school be-
cause she was the only one.
"I'm afraid she caught it round the
Buildings—from open dustbins, bad, smelly
drains, or dirty walls."
CASE TWO: Mrs. Bridget Sullivan, aged
26, wife of a factory worker, with children
Michael, 3, Theresa, one, in two rooms, no
kitchen, at £1 6s. 10d. a week. Her flat
is spotless.

TITLE: MEXICAN GIRLS HOE ON POOLSIDE
STORY: BEAUTY OF A MEXICAN VILLAGE

MEXICAN girls wearing huge straw hats hoe weeds
on the rim of a big pond in San Miguel Allende.
One is the daughter of Don Luis, owner of
the ranch. The other is the daughter of a hired
hand. That high adobe wall behind them is
part of a centuries old Hacienda, now belonging
to Americans. San Miguel Allende, Guanajuato,
Mexico, is an old charming little mountain
town, which is often said to be much more
European in character than is typical in this
continent. The flat cars are quite picturesque.
People here have big friendly smiles and are
polite, even to strangers. Many Americans, out
of work, have moved here to live very cheaply.
The San Miguel area, which was very unproductive
in the past, has recently received 40% government
subsidy for agriculture -- and many formerly
poor Mexicans, engaged in hand crafts, now
have big bank rolls. People work by an ancient
rule: 9:00AM on the job is considered late.
Life is simple and incredibly sweet.

XD) AUSTRALIAN BINDER AT WORK ON FORMER
PARKLAND. REMINDER OF A FORMER INVASION
THREAT.

Delving back into history when Europe was dominated
by Napoleon and England stood on the waiting list,
the fine old park lands at Bushy Park, Hampton,
Middlesex, were turned over to the needs of agricul-
ture and food production. After that period they
became park lands again up till to-day. Now
invasion threatens again and once more food production
must be served. To-day, the McKay Massey Harris
Sunshine Binder - new importation to this country
from Australia - is at work on the park lands: gave
interesting demonstrations to officials and Dominion
representatives. Fine oats are being grown on the
fields which were first ploughed up last November and
cross-harrowed in March. Yield is now 60-80 bushels p
per acre. Wheat and barley are also being grown.
The new binder, which should prove very satisfactory
to the English market, has a six-foot cut; refinements
include grease-gun pressure lubrication; gun-metal
bearings for the packers; enclosed oil-bath for the
main bevel gear drive. The big wheel is all metal,
wood is replaced in the decks by galvanized steel.
The sheaf carrier is simplicity itself.

Photo shows:- The horse team cutting the oats.
MR. A.R.MANTHYLLOW (Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries)
can be seen at back examining the cut.

HOUSE OF COMMONS GIFT TO RHODESIA AND

MACE IN THE MAKING

Craftsmen employed by a 74-years-old firm of London
silversmiths are now engaged on a task which is a
test of their skill - the production of the massive
mace to be presented by the House of Commons to the
new parliament for the Federation of Rhodesia and
Nyasaland. 100 ounces of silver are being used for
it and seven different categories of craftsmen are
putting their knowledge and skill into its
completion. 20 separate pieces are being soldered
together to make the finished piece. When completed
it will be 32 3/4 inches long. Nobody yet knows how
much the mace will weigh as it cannot be estimated
in advance how much gold will be required to guild
it. Only a single piece is being made to the design
and the craftsmen have no completed "article upon
which to base their calculations. The mace, which
is an exact replica in outline of the historic
House of Commons Mace, has been designed by Mr. R.H.
HILL, an instructor at the London County Council
Central School of Arts and Crafts.

WAR ON THE COLORADO BEETLE.
Drastic measures are being taken to combat the threat of invasion
of the Colorado beetle, and war has been declared by the authorities
responsible for the protection of the crops in Great Britain.
The agricultural areas around the airports, where aircraft from
overseas land, where potatoes are grown, are being sprayed as a
precaution against this pest.
Members of the National Fire Service are rendering valuable
assistance by carrying the water used to make the spray.
A solution of lead arsenate, deadly to the beetle but not harmful
to the crops, is sprayed over the halms of the potatoes from multi
jets at the back of the tractors.
The beetles stow away in aircraft from the Continent, and, as they
live only on potatoes, make for the nearest field of them.
These photographs were taken near Staines and Harmondsworth, to
the North and South of the London Airport at Heathrow.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The sprayers in action against the Colorado beetle
in a thirty acres field of potatoes in the Harmondsworth area.

Housing--Accidents--Flats Disaster at Canning Town,London
May 1968.
F S.N.A
MISS IVY HODGE (56)
in hospital
6 severe sms?

A GAS explosion in a kitchen
where a woman was making
a cup of tea is believed to
have caused yesterday's
collapse of skyscraper flats in
East London.
Three people died, and 11
were injured, as a wing of the
22-storey block broke away from
the rest of the building and
crashed to the ground "like a
pack of cards."
One of the injured was the
woman making a cup of tea, 56-
year-old Miss Ivy Hodge. Last
night she was recovering from face
burns in hospital.

As inquiries into the
collapse went on last
night scores of families
evacuated from the
block's 110 flats said they
never wanted to live in a
skyscraper flat again.

Mr. James Callaghan, the
Home Secretary, went to the
flats a few hours after the
collapse and appointed a
team of experts to make a
preliminary report to him by
lunchtime today.

At least three other in-
quiries will be held—one of
them by the Taylor Wood-
row firm who built the block,
and others like it, in the
London borough of Newham.

The cause of the explosion
was confirmed by Com-
mander Arthur Milbury,
head of the eastern area of
the London Fire Brigade.

He said: “There appears
to have been a gas explosion
in one of the flats. Gas fit-
tings were completely blown
away."

MISS IVY HODGE, the
woman who was making a
cup of tea when the ex-
plosion came, lay in a
hospital bed last night
(above) and told of her
miracle escape.

She said: "I had just
filled the kettle when I
suddenly found myself on
the floor.
"I managed to stagger
to the door and people
helped me down to safety."
Miss Hodge, who lives in
Flat 90 on the 18th floor,
said she could not remem-
ber turning on the gas or
striking a match.

A FULL-FLEDGED COOPER IN 1950

Amid the last of the craftsment to retain
their ancient customs and ceremonies is the
ancient trade of Cooperage and at the
Guinness Brewery, Park Royal, Apprentice
G.R.N. BANNER was literally "put through
the hoop" when he came out of his time
and became a full fledged cooper. First
he was dumped into a new barrel of his own
making, then shavings, coloured dyes, and
all the most obnoxious brewery material his
comrades could find, tipped over him. During
the pouring an "orchestra" of tubes, pipes
and pieces of metal kept up a continuous
clamour. Apprentice BANNER was then rolled the
full length of the Brewery at Park Royal.
After the rolling, he was permitted to "come
up for air", given a drink, and then "tossed
up" by his comrades. Still smiling, he
himself up and is "sacked" and re-
engaged by the Head Cooper in the status
of a fully qualified COOPER.

Apprentice G.R. BANNER emerges from his cocoon (barrel)
with a broad smile. He is almost a full fledged
cooper.

STANMORE POTTERS HOLD THEIR OWN EXHIBITION. NR/PM
Probably for the first time since it was made, about 5,000
years ago, a large Minoan vase is back in a pottery, for it
is the central exhibit in an exhibition in the Orchard Studio,
Stanmore-hill, Stanmore, now being staged by Mr and Mrs R.C.
Collyer. Mrs Collyer is better known as Pamela Nash. The Vase,
which is 20 inches high, 50 inches in circumference, and would
hold about four gallons of water, is made of a sandy-coloured
clay, and is decorated with the traditional spirals, or "bull's eyes"
of the period, which depicts the worship of the bull in the Palace
of Minos, in Knossos, Crete.

Photograph shows :- Mr and Mrs R.C. Collyer seen studying the
5,000 year old MINOAN VASE. Mrs Collyer is known as PAMELA NASH
who is an art painter and potter. She is seen holding the vase
while her husband is seen examining the design, and checking the design
with a reference book. It is on show at No.2 Stanmore Hill, Stanmore,

PEER TO VISIT PIT GIRLS.
HJB/VM

In reply to a challenge by Viscount Hall, arising out of
controversy over the second reading of the Mines and Quarries
Bill in the House of Lords, the Earl of Selkirk, Paymaster
General, is to spend part of his holidays touring collieries
to "see for himself" conditions under which the "pit brow
lassies" work. Viscount Hall declared that there were
still about 3,000 women employed at the pit tops in conditions
almost as bad as those prevailing at the time when women were
taken out of the pits nearly 100 years ago.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: A general view of "pit brow lassies" at
work on the screening of coal at Nickerpeece Colliery, Leigh,
near Manchester. Some of the women have been doing this work
for more than 20 years and all say that although the job is very
dirty, it is quite congenial. They work 8-hour shifts, 7 a.m.
to 3 p.m. or another shift finishing at 10.30 p.m. A modern
bath-house similar to the miners pithead bath is provided so that
the women can leave the colliery quite clean. Protective
clothing is also provided.

AUSTRALIAN PRIME MINISTER TO OPEN GAUR DAM
(pr. 17.6.53.
Mr ROBERT G. MENZIES, Prime Minister of Australia,
will open the Nth of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board's
new Dam and Power Station on the river Gaur, 3 miles
from Rannoch Station on the fringe of the dreaded moor
of Rannoch, in West Perthshire on June 20th.
The scheme is on the ancient lands of Glen Menzies, near
one of the few surviving parts of the old Caledonian Forest.
Loch Eigheach will be enlarged and raised 30' by a
crescent-shaped dam 40' high and 370' long. A 6,000 KW
power station on the River Gaur will produce 17 million
units of Electricity each year. The picture shows:-

No 1. The setting of the Gaur Dam showing Loch Eigheach
behind the rocky River Gaur in right foreground. The
ancient "Road to the Isles" now has a dam sitting on it
(see wall on right) and the road behind the dam will be
submerged. 1½ miles of new road has been built to take
its place.

FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS 18.12.46.

WINTER'S PROBLEM FOR WORLD'S BIGGEST GAS WORKS

Mr Shinwell's latest pronouncement on the coal situation
will have been received nowhere with greater interest than at the
Beckton plant of the Gas Light and Coke Company, of London, which
is the largest gasworks in the world. The works are capable of
producing daily 120 million cubic feet of gas equalling 600,000
therms, but actual production is, of course, dependent upon the
amount of coal available. Beckton is situated upon the North
bank of the Thames just East of the Royal Albert Dock, and has
a river frontage of 2500 ft for the handling of its coal, which
comes by water mainly from the coalfields of Durham. The works
cover 280 acres (540 acres including the adjoining chemical works)
and there are over 70 miles of full-guage railway tracks for
internal transport. The picture shows: Horizontal retort being
re-charged with coal by projector machine on other side of retort
bench. Stoker in foreground holds "stopper" in position to
regulate charge.

At the factory of the Standard Motor Co., the new Standard Eight car, will practically be which will be announced tomorrow. It is hoped that the workmanship shown in its construction will be exceptional and of a high standard. 

The new Standard Eight is from all parts of the world. The Standard Eight is a four door, four light, saloon, Blue, four speed gear box, which received advantages, and dual purpose, light weight, metal, radial tyres, etc. which are highly reliable and efficient. It is expected to be introduced next year, and will be a significant success for the company. 

A number of 4000 cars are already on order and the company intends to produce 10,000 cars per year at the start. 

The car will be available in a number of colours and finishes, including red, blue, green, and black. The interior will be finished in leather and the seats will be upholstered in cloth. The car will also come with a number of optional extras, including air conditioning, a sunroof, and a stereo system. 

The new Standard Eight is expected to be a major competitor in the compact car market. It is hoped that it will be a success.

Com. say the new Standard Eight car, full details of

Mrs. V. Tudor, daughter

So my plans for a holiday in

and plan to do a lot of sight-seeing.
We are not worried about the cold
weather in Europe, as we will have
our warmest clothes with us.

Queen + Duke

WHEN you're only 23
months old, nobody's
going to mind very much if
you're a little informal with
Royalty.
Wee Jimmy Smith, wearing
his best velvet trousers, left
stuffy ceremony to the older
folk yesterday and showed the
Queen how pleased he was to
see her.
While his father, Sergeant
Harry Smith, stood to attention
outside his R.A.F. home at
Leuchars, Fife, Jimmy advanced
smartly. Result: The picture
above.
Jimmy, a lad of few words,
had two for her Majesty:
HELLO, QUEEN.
He held on to the Queen's
hand and did an impromptu
war-dance while she laughed
and chatted to him.
That was the warm, unex-
pected incident in a duty-packed
day for the Queen and the Duke
of Edinburgh.
It was a day of new experi-
ences for the Queen, too. She
had her first 450 m.p.h. jet plane
flight—in a Comet II—from
Marham to Leuchars.
As the plane brought the
Queen to earth, men of the
famous 43 Squadron stood ready
for the presentation of their
blue and gold standard.
Another thrilling moment for
the Queen was when she took
over the microphone of the air
control tower at Leuchars.
She ordered two lines of
fighters to "scramble."

THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404-3 (BKS-R)
---------------------------------------
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE

For at least seven centuries, the manufacture
of nets, ropes, sailcloth and other hempen
products has been the staple industry of
the town of Bridport, Dorset.
Of Bridport's present-day population of about
6,000, over a thousand - many of them young
women - are engaged in the industry,
directly or indirectly.
At one time locally-grown flax and hemp were
used, but nearly all the raw material is
now imported.
It is recorded that all the ropes and sails
for King John's Navy (he reigned from
1199-1216) were made at Bridport. And the
expression 'stabbed by a Bridport dagger' for
a person who had been hanged was current
in 1530, when King Henry VIII reigned.
This picture was taken in the Bridport works
of Joseph Gundry and Co. Ltd., a firm founded
in 1665 and still controlled by lineal
descendants of the founder. There were
Gundrys engaged in the trade as early as 1580.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Two of the girls in the
Bridport net trade - ARINA RUNDELL (left)
and SHIRLEY WARD - rigging seine fishing-net
25 yards long. It will fish to a depth
of eight feet.

ROYAL PRESENT FOR KING OF THAILAND.
26.4.50.

For their wedding present to the King of Thailand
their Majesties, have chosen a service of Worcester Royal
Porcelain. The pattern chosen is known as the Royal Lily
Pattern and is printed in underglaze blue and enriched with
gold. The design was originally adapted from the Chinese at
the Worcester factory between 1751 and 1788, and was selecte
by King George III and Queen Charlotte when they visited the
works in 1788. Throughout its 200 years history, the Worceste
factory has produced distinguished underglaze blues. The
Worcester factory was one of the first to be established in
England when, in the middle of the eighteenth century,
European potters were discovering how to produce porcelain
similar to the Chinese ware, and its early products rank wi
those of Bow and Chelsea in the "Golden age" of English
porcelain. The craftsmanship inherited from those days ha
helped to produce this royal present.

1983-5236/57047

"GRAVEYARD OF GIANTS"
WHERE BATTLESHIPS GO FOR SCRAP DG/PR

"Abandon Hope All Ye That Enter Here" is the ironic
warning over the entrance to the jetty of Messrs.
Thomas Ward, shipbreakers, of Inverkeithing,
Scotland, and so far as warships are concerned, the
phrase applies down to the last rivet.
Wards are the biggest shipbreakers in Britain, and
one of the largest in the world. Not only are they
the biggest shipbreakers, but they break up the
biggest ships. To their yards--and to others
such as Metal Industrials, or Arnott and Young's--
come such floating giants as "Rodney", "Revenge",
"Renown", the "New York", once Hitler's "strength
through joy" liner, and many others. Mighty fighting
ships which sailed triumphantly through two world
wars, find their last resting place under scrapyard
cranes. Guns which the combined fleets of
the Third Reich and Imperial Japanese Navy failed
to muffle, are silent as hissing oxy-acetylene
cutters carve into their vitals.
Much of the valuable scrap goes to sea again in
the form of new ships, and thus fights in Britain's
export drive. Brass, copper and much needed alloys
are sent to Sheffield, while metal scrap goes to
Newcastle.

H.M.S. Royal Sovereign, showing her forward turrets,
at T. Ward's scrapyard.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY
GK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co, of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

WILSON FAMILY BUILD THEIR OWN HOUSE AT GRAVESEND -
DAD SWITCHED FROM BEAUFIGHTING TO BRICKLAYING.

Convinced that the only way to get a house in these days
of building shortages is to built it oneself,
ex-Beaufighter radio operator W. Wilson of Parrock Street,
Gravesend, Kent, has set about erecting his own home
in Milton Hall Road, Gravesend.
Released from the Royal Air Force two years ago and now
a foreman bricklayer, Mr. Wilson has enrolled his wife
(a State Registered Nurse) and their two children,
Robin, 5, and Frances, 3, in the project.
Mrs.Wilson claims she can mix a heap of concrete as well
as any professional, while Robin and Frances make good use
of their wheelbarrow (carrying capacity: three bricks).
Construction work is carried on in the evenings and at
week-ends. In one week-end the Wilson family laid
a total of 1,750 bricks.

R.F.D.

The photograph shows for the first time the phenomenon
known as 'aquaplaning'. The duality technician is testing a
smooth tyre which, although under an 800 lb. load, remains
stationary while the drum beneath revolves at 30 m.p.h. The
tyre remains stationary because a thin film of water has penetrated
between the drum and the tyre, giving the tyre no grip or contact
with the rough surface of the drum.

The amount of water sprayed on to the drum, 6 gallons
per minute, is considerably less than the 8-10 pints per second
that a tyre would have to cope with at 30 m.p.h. on a wet road.
At speeds below 45 m.p.h. the tyre revolved at the same speed as
the drum, but thereafter, as the drum speed increased and as the
grip became less and less, the tyre slowed down until at between
40 and 50 m.p.h. it stopped rotating and 'aquaplaned'.

Driving with smooth tyres on wet roads involves serious
and unwarranted risks to the driver and other road users alike.

Transcribed_Text:
STANDSTILL AT 80 M.P.H.

The photograph shows for the first time the phenomenon
known as 'aquaplaning'. The Dunlop technician is touching a
smooth tyre which, although under an 800 lb. load, remains
stationary while the drum beneath revolves at 80 m.p.h. The
tyre remains stationary because a thin film of water has penetrated
between the drum and the tyre, giving the tyre no grip or contact
with the rough surface of the drum.

The amount of water sprayed on to the drum, 6 gallons
per minute, is considerably less than the 8 - 10 pints per second
that a tyre would have to cope with at 50 m.p.h. on a wet road.
At speeds below 45 m.p.h. the tyre revolved at the same speed as
the drum, but thereafter, as the drum speed increased and as the
grip became less and less, the tyre slowed down until at between
60 and 80 m.p.h. it stopped rotating and 'aquaplaned'.

Driving with smooth tyres on wet roads involves serious
and unwarranted risks to the driver and other road users alike.

WAR ON THE COLORADO BEETLE.

Drastic measures are being taken to combat the threat of invasion
of the Colorado beetle,and war has been declared by the authorities
responsible for the protection of the crops in Great Britain.
The agricultural areas around the airports, where aircraft from
overseas land, where potatoes are grown, are being sprayed as a
precaution against this pest.
Members of the National Fire Service are rendering valuable
assistance by carrying the water used to make the spray.
A solution of lead arsenate, deadly to the beetle but not harmful
to the crops, is sprayed over the halms of the potatoes from multi
jets at the back of the tractors.
The beetles stow away in aircraft from the Continent, and, as they
live only on potatoes, make for the nearest field of them.
Those photographs were taken near Staines and Harmondsworth, to
the North and South of the London Airport at Heathrow.

special tanks of lead arsenate mounted on the spraying tractors,

DAILY HERALD Feb. 25 1955 7

Tenants get 'buy or rent rise' threat

A PROPOSAL has been made to four tenants of a tenement in Wellington-street, Dundee, that they buy their houses—or pay a 40 per cent. rent increase.
One tenant, Mr. John Macbeth, aged 60, was told on a postcard from the landlord's agent, Mr. George J. Lindsay, a Dundee pharmacist:—
"You will note we have not yet added the permitted increase of 40 per cent. to the rents—but we are considering doing so after May term. "Meantime, should you wish to purchase the house before May 28, the price will be £200.
"After May the price will be based on the increased rental. The increase in your case will be 25s. per quarter."
The three other tenants have been told verbally of the landlord's plan.

PROPER WAY
Dundee's chief sanitary inspector, Mr. W. M. Smith, said yesterday: "A rent increase under the Housing and Repairs Act must be submitted to the tenant on the prescribed form, giving details of the proposed increase, the work undertaken and the amount spent over a specified period.
"It is not legal to do it verbally."
Mr. Lindsay, of Castle-street, Dundee, said: "This is a private matter. There is an Act which allows increases.
"I have done nothing yet. If anything is to be done it will be done legally."

DAILY HERALD
25 FEB 1955

SAFETY MASKS HAVE GLAMOUR NOW

GLAMOUR goes hand in hand with safety in the new protective masks shown in these two pictures.
They are the latest type of protective wear for factory workers and they will be shown, along with other specially-designed protective clothing, at an out-of-the-ordinary fashion display in London at the end of the month.
The show, part of an exhibition of factory equipment at the Royal Horticultural Hall, aims to prove that girls who do a tough job can still look feminine and attractive.

THE BATTLE goes on non-stop. Throughout the day and long into the night.
For Britain's farm workers, like these at Space Farm in West Horsley, Surrey, it is a battle to gather the remnants of their storm-thrashed harvest.
Farmer Percy Yates, who has been working in the glare of arc lamps and tractor lights, cannot remember a more difficult harvest: "We have had to work hard in appalling conditions."
He added: "We have had to take advantage of every minute during the last few days of fine weather."
"But the fields are soggy from all the rain and the corn has been beaten down. It is very hard to combine and it is thick with weeds and grass."

Excellent

At the headquarters of the National Farmers' Union in Knightsbridge, cold statistics tell the story: Somerset, only 30 per cent. of the harvest in. Wiltshire, only 50 per cent.
Said an official: "Men are harvesting in paddy field conditions. The whole harvest is two to three weeks behind.
"Even in places like Cornwall, where they have got 85 per cent. of the harvest in, the grain is light and the yield is below average."
The long-range weather forecast is far from heartening: "Cool, disturbed and occasional stormy weather. Intervals of more settled weather are likely to be brief. Rainfall totals are likely to exceed the average."
Provisional estimates for the 1965 harvest are considerably lower than last year when the good summer yielded excellent crops.

SILAS leans out of a window, torch in hand, Bambi beside him, as a caller arrives.
Son, ordered out of house, stays with two dogs
THE SIEGE OF Chatsworth Road
Express Staff Reporter
SILAS ("Let 'em all come") Bentley is waiting for 10 o'clock this morning. For that is the hour at which he has been told by the local council to quit a house owned by his father.
West Ham Council wants to put in more tenants at 5, Chatsworth-road, Forest Gate, which it requisitioned in 1940. The last tenant moved out 10 weeks ago.
Last night 25-year-old Silas was at heavily bolted No. 5. Determined, he said, to stay. And with him were dogs Bambi, a Boxer, and Jack, a Manchester terrier.
Silas's father, Mr. Charles Bentley, made frequent requests for his son to be allowed to move into the house. To each the council said "No."
Yesterday Silas got on a bicycle at his father's shop in nearby Forest-street and pedalled with his bed on his shoulders to Chatsworth-road.
Bambi and Jack followed him yelping. The Bentley family—mother, father, sister, niece, and nephew—brought up the rear.
They carried Silas's provisions for a possible siege—five tins of meat, three tins of dog food, two tins of peaches ("I'm fond of peaches"), and four loaves of bread.
Silas came to a bedroom window to answer questions last night. The dogs began barking. It was two minutes before they stopped.
Who goes there?
Silas, a burly, curly-headed, 5ft. 8in. figure, called down, "Who goes there?"
I said I was a reporter. There was no answer. I did not have the password.
Silas's mother came to the rescue. She stumped round the corner crying "Cuckoo." This was the signal. I walked in behind Mrs. B. The dogs bounded forward. Silas shouted: "Stop." I breathed again.
"It is my father's house. I am his tenant, and here I am staying," said Silas.
"My wife Myrtle, for whom I had no home is coming up from Devon to join me."
"How long do you think you can last out?" I asked.
"A long, long time," replied Silas.

HOG, WATER. Ploughing with an 80-h.p. track-type tractor in 1935 was one of the first ploughing and soil erosion experiments used in Texas. The agricultural engineers are now giving farmers the benefits of the very latest implements. During 1934, they were still using a few years older implements which did not fit the Blacklands very well, although using a field much larger than the average. This field was large and fairly level. One of the greatest problems is erosion by wind and water. The cultivated area has been a level-terraced field for 10 years, and there is a 30-foot drop from the cultivating area to the outlet of the terraces. Nobody knows for certain how the field was levelled, but one man on the county remembers the plowing for not more than 50 years.
Before being cultivated by Harley, cultivating the land with a 6-foot lister, was a contract between him and the landowner who will harvest the sorghum and oats by hand. 24448

London: An industrial project which has aroused
much controversy from the time of its conception
has just gone into operation.
It is the Bankside Power Station, at which
the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator of about
80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the power station was so strong that
in January, 1947, a public inquiry was held, with the
result that the scheme was given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will
comprise four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the
oil consumption at full load (16-hour day) being
67 tons an hour, consuming in one winter's day about
850 tons.

THE first all-in working-class
flat estate in this country—
a model village in storeys—
opened by Sir Kingsley Wood,
Minister for Health, in North
Kensington, yesterday, has:—
A nursery school, separate club-
rooms for children and the grown-
ups, workshops, playgrounds, a
concert-platform and a canteen.
Its 379 inhabitants have been salvaged
from some of the worst slums in London
—those of the Royal Borough of
Kensington—by the Gas Light and Coke
Company.
The company, operating as the Capitol
Housing Association, set out to prove
that it was possible to give working-class
people social amenities enjoyed by the
wealthier middle-class at costs they could
afford.
Rent for a three-bedroom flat is 11s. 6d.
including rates, and for a two-bedroom
only 9s. 6d.
Sixty children on the estate who are
under five are looked after by nursery-
school experts and given their meals—
all for 3d. a day, with an extra penny
for cod-liver oil.
The well-being of the community is
supervised by an executive committee of
the tenants — two representatives for
each of the seven staircases. A caretaker
looks after the general tidiness.

The plant was to have been officially opened today, but the ceremony has been postponed because of labour troubles which have affected the brewery since production started.
Earlier this month work was stopped when staff went on strike in protest at delays in pay discussions.
Yesterday a management official said: "We are involved in talks with the unions.
"We are anxious not to do anything to upset the talks."
We'll drink to that.

THE Devices were there two years ago when Mr. Burdett took the house; have been there, in fact, for 30 years.
Well, about Coronation time the Middlesex County Council said: "What about paying the armorial bearings duty?"
Mr. Burdett refused to pay, and the Council twice hailed him before the court.
Once the case was dismissed under the Probation of Offenders Act; the second time he was fined.
Still he refused to pay, maintaining that his Devices were not, as the Bench said, armorial bearings.
* * *
SO now the Middlesex County Council has decided to press the County Councils' Association to ask for the abolition of the duty.

'TROLLEYBUS' TRACTOR GETS FIRST TRY-OUT

Reading, Berkshire: Something new in farming machinery is
the 'trolley-bus' tractor, an electric device invented by
Russian scientists, and now being tried for the first time in
this country.
The miniature tractor, seen being operated by 17-year-old Yvonne
Shepheard, has no engine. It is driven instead by a simple
electric motor powered from the mains. A strong, thin cable
links the tractor with a wooden pylon in the middle of the
market garden. The cable is automatically paid out as the
girl drives away. Counterweights take up the slack as she returns.
The scientists at the Electrical Research Association Laboratory
near Reading, who are testing the garden 'trolley bus', claim it
has three outstanding advantages over an engine-powered tractor:-
It is much cheaper to run. It needs less attention and is almost
free from breakdowns. It is much more powerful for its size.

1983-5236 / 53560 .

NEW CREPE & RAYON INDUSTRY IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
A new industry which has sprung up in Northern
Ireland is the preparation and weaving of
rayon crepe and other rayon fabrics.
Crepe Weavers Ltd., of Newtownards, Co. Down,
which commenced in 1948 occupies part of Newtownards
Airport which was originally built for the production
of aircraft.
It employs 125 people at present but will employ
200 people by the end of the year when the mill is
fully equipped.
Owing to the male unemployment situation in the
district it is the intention of the firm to employ
60 per cent men and 40 per cent women.
The production target for the end of the year is
30,000 yards of Rayon fabrics per week, of which
between 50 and 60% will be for export.
Most of the workers engaged are trainees formerly
agricultural labourers and laundry workers.
Care has been taken not to engage workers from linen
textile mills in the district which would have added
to the production of the new firm but would have
caused difficulties in the established firms.

EIDER DUCK SCHOOL.

The spring season for jam-nut fishing on the Eider River has begun, and we are told that despite the long hours it has yielded so far, there are still some days left to the start of the season. Although much larger catches are expected at this time of year, owing to the development of the rather elaborate "jam-nut fishing" system, which was developed over the last 20 years, the Eider River has been experiencing rather light catches this season. Jam-nut fishing is a method of catching fish by means of a string of bait, which is cast out into the river and then drawn in by means of a pulley. The bait is generally composed of fish spawn, but other forms of bait may also be used. The jam-nut fishing system is rather elaborate, and it is said to be quite effective in catching fish. However, it is also said to be quite difficult to learn, and it is not recommended for beginners.

LIFE AT THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.

Christ's Hospital or "Blue Coat School", was founded by
Edward VI on the site of an old Greyfriars Monastery, and down
to a few years ago was one of London's best known scholastic
institutions. It was pulled down to make room for extensions
of St. Bartholomew's Hospital and the new General Post Office,
in Newgate Street. The School is now carried on at HORSHAM in
an imposing building. Besides the usual subjects included in
any school curriculum, the boys are taught intersting things,
such as clay modelling, carpentry, weaving, spinning etc., and
have taken advantage of their move into the country by acquiring
a farm, the work on which is done by the boys. The school has
a band complete with mace bearer and this is a familiar sight
once a year in London when the school marches through the City to
their annual church service. The boys still wear the picturesque
costume of knee breeches, yellow stockings and blue coats.

lord’s agent.
“Is that so?” replied Mrs.
Esther Clara Garrett, of Irene
House, Flower and Dean-street,
Whitechapel, E.
She is the chairwoman of the
committee formed by 180 tenants of
tenements there, to demand rent re-
ductions and repairs.
With no schooling except that
which comes from going to work at
eight years of age and bringing up a
large family, Mrs. Garrett yesterday
made her first “public appearance.”
She left the two-room flat for
which she pays 13s. a week rent and
spoke to 250 men, women and
children.
They cheered as she told them,
“I’ll go to the landlord and whatever
there is to say, I’ll say it.”
The meeting followed a procession
from Flower and Dean-street, with
drums playing and banners flying.
Organised by the Stepney Tenants’
Defence League, the meeting decided
to send the landlord a suggested
scale of rents and repairs, with a rent
strike ultimatum if there is no satis-
faction or negotiation in seven days.

An Aluminium House. Factory-made in four sections, has been put up on a bombed site outside Balfour's, the departmental store in Oxford-street, London. The lightweight hope, which may play an important part in the solution of Britain's housing problem, was designed by the Aircraft Industries Research Organisation on Housing, and built by the Bristol Aeroplane Company, of Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, and is called the Airch House. Electrical fittings are installed when the sections are constructed, being plugged in to the mains after assembly. Which can be completed in four hours. Production of the Airch House in aircraft factories ensures continuity of employment for skilled workers in aluminium, hitherto employed on making parts for aeroplanes, besides meeting a national demand for homes to replace those destroyed in the war.

RELIC OF THE "RODNEY"
IN THE GRAVEYARD OF SHIPS               DC/PR

To few sailors falls the privilage of seeing
both the first days and the last of      their
ships. Chief Petty Officer pensioner ROBERT G.
ELLIS (58) can , however make this boast. A
member of the staff of Britain's biggest ship-
breakers (Thomas Ward, Inverkeithing,Scotland)
Mr. Ellis joined H.M.S. Rodney when she was first
commissioned at Devonport and is now standing by
her as she is broken up . In his 34 years 19
days in the Royal Navy Mr. Ellis served in
two world wars . He fought at Jutland and has
memories of Admiral Cunningham-then a Lieutenant,
now C.in C. Rosyth. In this recent war, Mr.
Ellis was a Landing Craft Instructor to Commandos.

PHOTO SHOWS: With overalls and cap replacing his
naval uniform, Mr. ELLIS, now crane maintenance
man, holds up the nameplate of the battleship
Rodney, a relic he hopes to keep as a souvenir.
Pall of smoke in background is from burning oil
sludge removed to facilitate cutting operations
on the battleship's hull.

DAILY HER
30 DEC 1960
MRS. D. ANDERSON
"A car, holidays"

WIVES go out to work first and foremost because they want the money.
But they do not usually need it for basic necessities. Nor do they spend it as "pin-money" on themselves.
They want it so that their families can have a higher standard of living than is possible on one wage alone. And if a conflict arises between the claims of their jobs and the interests of their families, they put their families first.
This new evidence on the con-troversial subject of working wives and mothers is put for-ward today in a report published by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research.
It is based on a study of mar-ried women workers, sponsored by the DSIR, and carried out by social scientists from the London School of Economics under Professor R. M. Titmuss, at the Peek Frean biscuit factory in Bermondsey, London.
At this factory, three-quarters of the 4,000 workers are women—most of them married, more than half of them with children. Few work the full 10-hour day. Most are part-timers on shifts of 4, 5 or 6½ hours.

NOT AN ESCAPE
The investigators found that for most wives "work was un-dertaken as a means of helping the family, not as an escape from it."
Two pay-packets in the family mean that more can be spent on refurnishing the home, on more varied food, on pocket-money and toys for the children, on a small, second-hand car or on a proper family holiday.
Though many wives said they would miss the social contacts if they did not work, their first loyalty was always to their families.
The biscuit factory—abandon-

By JOYCE CHESTERTON
ing its pre-war bar against married women because of the labour shortage — has done much to make it easier for wives to work.
The 9.30 a.m.-4 p.m. shift, for instance, consists mainly of mothers with school-age chil-dren. They can leave home and get back at the same time as their families.
Mothers with under-fives work mostly in the evening, when husbands are at home to take over and put the children to bed.
Without considerable help from husbands, in fact, most of the wives would find it very hard to cope with both job and home.

launched today, Thursday, at the Belfast Ship-

Oom, wife of the managing director of Regent

Liverpool" is the 218th vessel in the Regent/
Texaco/Caltex Group fleet which links a world
wide network of more than 80 ocean terminals.

that Regent plans to build at Milford Haven.

LONDON SCHOOLS' CHRISTMAS FESTIVAL BEGINS. MJH/HA.

The first concert of the 1955 London Schools' Christmas Carol
Festival, is taking place today at the Central Hall, Westminster.
A massed choir of some 16,000 children from more than 550 schools
in all parts of London are taking part in this Festival, which
comprises a series of six concerts, on December 6th, 7th.
8th, 9th, 12th, and 13th., the first two being held at
the Central Hall and the last four at the Royal Festival Hall.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Six young choristers seen taking part
in the first concert of the London Schools' Christmas Carol
Festival at the Central Hall, Westminster this morning.
They are (back row left to right): CHARLES PAGE (11) from
Burdett Coutts School; BABLU MUKHERJI of Colville School,
Kensington(11); PAMELA DUNCAN, COLVILLE School, (10);
Front row: MARY JANE MILNER (10) of Highgate; OWEN MASON (10)
Westbourne Park: ANN RUMALRES (11) of Eltham.
The concerts are all conducted by Dr. Leslie Russell, the L.C.C's

They’re shining up partizans
and axes

GLITTERING swords . . . shining partizans and axes . . . they’ll all play their part in the grand pageantry of the Coronation next year.
And at the Acton, Middlesex, factory of the famous sword makers, Wilkinsons, 1,000 swords are being made for Guardsmen, Cavalrymen, Lord Lieutenants of Counties, diplomats, statesmen and officers of the three services.
Hundreds of other swords, handed down for generations, are being repaired and repolished.
Mrs. Mary Fry (in the picture below) is seen giving the final polish to some of the completed swords. In another small room, Charlie Webb, 39-year-old embosser, works on thep artizans—the broad spear-heads carried on tasseled poles by Yeomen of the Guard and Yeomen Wardens of the Tower.
He is cleaning off the late King’s arms and cypher and re-etching them with those of Queen Elizabeth. He is also regilding the axes carried by the Gentlemen at Arms.
★
SIX Prime Ministers will attend a meeting of the Coronation Commission at St. James’s Palace on Friday. The Duke of Edinburgh will preside.
In addition to Mr. Churchill they are the Prime Ministers of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Pakistan, and Ceylon, who were all appointed members of the Commission when it was set up in April.
Friday’s meeting probably will discuss the part the Commonwealth forces will play at the Coronation and also the question of television.
It is likely to be the only meeting that the Prime Ministers can attend, although their High Commissioners are also members of the Commission.
★
WORKMEN yesterday moved into Westminster Abbey to begin preparing it for the Coronation. The nave and west door are now closed to the public.
The public will be allowed in for services up to and including Christmas, but the whole Abbey will be closed from January 1.
Five days after the Coronation the public will be able to visit the Abbey to see the Coronation trappings.

BARGE FULL OF EELS
TO HOLD FLOATING EELS.
36/83

The home of 100,000 live eels, a barge full of
eels, has been built in Essex. The barge will
be moored at Heybridge Basin, Malden. The barge
named the "Johan" is believed to be the first of its
kind to be built in this country. The owner is
Mr. N.D. Ruijten, an importer of live eels.
The centre part of the barge is perforated
so that water can flow in freely. Watertight
compartments support the craft fore and aft, with
the deck no more than 10 inches above water
level. Fifty tons of eels will live in the

The following is a report on the present condition of the U.S. Navy's
Sea Water Distillation Program.

The Multi-Stage Flash Distillation (MSF) program,
which is being built at the Brooklyn Navy Yard and for
the Newport Naval Base, is progressing according to schedule.
The Newport installation will have a capacity
equivalent to launching thirty million gallons per day.
The Brooklyn Navy Yard will have a total capacity of
sixty million gallons per day. The MSF units are
expected to go into operation in October, 1968.

The MSF units will be capable of distilling
salt water by using the heat generated from nuclear
reactors. The purpose of this program is to make the
U.S. Navy less dependent on shore-based facilities
for fresh water. The units will also be able to produce
up to ten thousand gallons of distilled water per day,
which can be used for drinking, cooking, and other
household purposes. The U.S. Navy is committed to the
successful completion of this program.

NORTH SEA WEATHER CONDITIONS. THE RIG WILL BE TOWED BY
OCEAN-GOING TUGS TO THE NORTH SEA DRILLING SITE, AND WILL
THEN LOWER THE FOUR LEGS TO THE SEA BED. EQUIPPED WITH
THE LATEST TYPE OF DRILLING MACHINERY, THE RIG WILL BE
ABLE TO DRILL DOWN TO 20,000 FEET BENEATH THE SEA.

Indus- Fuel & Power- Coal--Accidents- Cambrian Colliery, Rhonda,
May 1965
AN explosion tore through a colliery yesterday and blasted 31 men to pieces. Last night, as the Rhondda Valley lay silent and numbed with shock, the cause of the disaster was still a mystery.
Weeping wives and mothers stood at the pit-head of Cambrian Colliery in Clydach Vale, Glamorgan, as the remains of their men were brought out of the black hell 800ft. below.
It was lunchtime when the blast hit the mechanised plough face of the colliery’s No. 1 Pit.
The miners working there had no chance. Men 500 yards away were knocked off their feet and injured.
The doomed men were in a slender tunnel only 2ft. 8in. high.
A grey-faced, shaken rescue worker said: “The sight down there was terrible.
“Some men were decapitated, others without arms and legs. Their clothing was ripped to shreds.”
Among the dead were colliery manager Ernest Breeze and under-manager Les Williams.
